docs.title: L22 · Files & directories (the API)
docs.text:
Book: Ch 39 (pp. 457–476) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 40 min

In plain words

Under the hood, a file is a numbered box of bytes. The number is the inode number. A directory is a list matching friendly names to those numbers, like a phone's contacts mapping "Mum" to a number.

  • open gives you a file descriptor, a ticket for "this open file". Keep it for reading and writing.
  • write usually only reaches memory at first. fsync means "really put it on the disk now".
  • A name is just a link to the box, and a box can have several names. Deleting a name (unlink) removes the box only when no names, and no open tickets, are left.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• A file is a linear array of bytes with a low-level name, the inode number. A directory is a file that maps human names → inode numbers.
  • open() returns a file descriptor (a per-process handle); each open has its own offset in the system-wide open file table. write() usually goes to memory first — fsync() forces it to disk.
  • A name is just a link to an inode. link() adds a hard link (refcount++), unlink() removes one; the file is deleted when the count hits 0. Symbolic links are files holding a path — they can dangle.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How should the OS manage a persistent device? What should the API look like, and what are its important aspects?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Need named, persistent data → files (bytes + inode number) and directories (name → inode) → open → fd → read/write with a current offset → lseek to move the offset → ❌ write returns before the data is on disk → fsync() (and fsync the directory for a new file) → ❌ how to update a file atomically? → write a temp file, fsync, rename() over the old one (rename is atomic) → names are links; deleting = unlink → ❌ hard links can't cross file systems or point to directories → symbolic links.

docs.title: File descriptors and offsets
docs.text:
When a program opens a file, three layers are involved. The program gets a small number (the file descriptor, e.g. 3). That number points to an entry in the OS's open file table, which remembers how far through the file you are (the offset). That entry points to the file's inode, which holds its size and where its data is on disk.

flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Process A"]
        fd3a["fd 3"]
    end
    subgraph P2["Process B (child after fork)"]
        fd3b["fd 3"]
    end
    subgraph OFT["Open file table (system-wide)"]
        e1["entry: offset=10, refcnt=2, R/W"]
    end
    fd3a --> e1
    fd3b --> e1
    e1 --> I["inode 1234"]
  • Each open() creates a new entry with its own offset, even for the same file. Open a file twice and you can read the start and the end independently.
  • After fork() (or dup()), the parent's and child's descriptors point to the same entry, so they share one offset. If the child reads 10 bytes, the parent's next read starts 10 bytes further on. (The entry keeps a count of how many descriptors use it, so it's freed only when the last one closes.)
  • The offset moves forward as you read or write, or you can set it directly with lseek(). Despite the name, lseek only changes a number in memory; the disk arm doesn't move.

docs.title: Key calls
docs.text: Call Does open(path, flags, mode) Opens (or creates) a file and returns a file descriptor. Flags say how: O_CREAT = create if missing, O_WRONLY = write only, O_TRUNC = empty it first read(fd, buf, n) / write(fd, buf, n) Read or write up to n bytes at the current offset, then move the offset forward lseek(fd, off, whence) Jump to a position in the file fsync(fd) "Put everything I've written on the disk now, and only return when it's there" rename(old, new) Rename a file. It happens all at once (atomically), even across a crash: you see either the old name or the new one, never a broken half stat(path) / fstat(fd) Get a file's details: size, owner, permissions, times, number of links mkdir, opendir, readdir, rmdir Make, list and remove directories (rmdir only works on an empty one) link(old, new) / unlink(path) Add or remove a name for a file symlink (shell: ln -s) Create a symbolic link (shortcut) mount Attach another file system (e.g. a USB stick) at a folder in the tree

docs.title: Hard vs symbolic links
docs.text: Hard link Symbolic link What it is A second name for the very same file (same inode) A small separate file that just contains a path, like a Windows shortcut Delete the original name The file survives, since it still has another name The link now points at nothing (dangling link) Can point to another disk/partition ✘ ✔ Can point to a directory ✘ (could create loops in the tree) ✔

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
In ls -l, you see strings like -rwxr-x---. After the first character (the file type), it's three groups of three: what the owner, the group and everyone else may do. r = read, w = write, x = execute (run it, or, for a directory, enter it). So rwxr-x--- means: owner can do everything, group can read and run, others can do nothing. More detailed per-user rules are called ACLs (access control lists).

A classic security bug (TOCTTOU, "time of check to time of use"): a program checks a file is safe (stat) and then opens it. In the gap between the two, an attacker swaps the file for something else.

docs.title: Atomic file update recipe
docs.text:
fd = open("foo.txt.tmp", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0644);
write(fd, buf, size);
fsync(fd);
close(fd);
rename("foo.txt.tmp", "foo.txt");    // atomic swap

Why this works: you never touch the real foo.txt until the very end. You write the new version to a temporary file, make sure it's really on disk (fsync), then rename swaps it into place in one step. If the power fails at any point, foo.txt is either the complete old version or the complete new one, never half-written. Text editors save files this way.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• write() returning doesn't mean the data is on disk.
  • lseek() doesn't cause disk I/O.
  • rm calls unlink() — it only removes a name; the inode goes when refcount (and open fds) reach 0.
  • Two opens of one file = two offsets; fork/dup = one shared offset.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the fd → open file table → inode picture; hard vs soft link table; the atomic-update recipe.

What is an inode number?

The file's low-level name; the file system uses it to find the inode (metadata and block pointers).

What does a directory contain?

A list of (name, inode number) pairs, including "." and "..".

When do two file descriptors share an offset?

When they refer to the same open-file-table entry: after fork() or dup(). Separate open() calls get separate offsets.

Why call fsync()?

write() buffers data in memory; fsync forces it (and metadata) to persistent storage.

How do you update a file atomically?

Write a temporary file, fsync it, then rename() it over the original; rename is atomic.

Hard link vs symbolic link?

Hard link: another name for the same inode (refcount). Symlink: a file containing a path; can cross file systems and point to directories, but can dangle.

Why is the call to remove a file named unlink()?

It removes one name (link) to the inode; the file is freed only when the link count drops to zero.

docs.title: L23 · File system implementation (VSFS)
docs.text:
Book: Ch 40 (pp. 477–493) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 55 min · Simulator: file-implementation/vsfs.py

In plain words

The disk is a giant shelf of numbered blocks (4 KB each). A simple file system splits it into zones:

  • Superblock: the label on the shelf. How big it is and where everything starts.
  • Bitmaps: two checklists of which inodes and which data blocks are free.
  • Inode table: one card per file, with its size, owner, times and which blocks hold its data.
  • Data blocks: the actual contents.

Opening /home/notes.txt means: read the root folder's card → find "home" → read home's card → find "notes.txt" → read its card → now you know where the data is. That's several disk reads, which is why the OS caches heavily in memory.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• A simple file system divides the disk into blocks (4 KB): superblock · inode bitmap · data bitmap · inode table · data region.
  • An inode holds metadata and pointers to data: direct pointers, then indirect (and double/triple indirect) blocks — a tree tuned for "most files are small".
  • Opening /foo/bar reads the root inode, root data, foo's inode, foo's data, bar's inode — one hop per path component. Caching (page cache) hides reads; write buffering batches writes.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we build a simple file system? What structures are needed on disk, and what do they track?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Need to store files on a block device → data region + inode table → track what's free: bitmaps → superblock describes the layout → inode needs to point to blocks → a few direct pointers → ❌ big files → indirect blocks (then double/triple) → directories are files of (name, inum) → ❌ every open/read/write costs several I/Os → cache blocks in memory (unified page cache) + delay and batch writes (5–30 s) → ❌ batching risks data loss on crash → fsync, and crash consistency (L25).

docs.title: On-disk layout (64 blocks example)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["S<br/>superblock<br/>(block 0)"] --- IB["i<br/>inode<br/>bitmap"] --- DB["d<br/>data<br/>bitmap"] --- IT["I I I I I<br/>inode table<br/>(blocks 3–7)"] --- D["D D D … D<br/>data region<br/>(blocks 8–63)"]
  • 4 KB blocks, 256-byte inodes → 16 inodes per block → 5 blocks = 80 inodes max.
  • Superblock: number of inodes and data blocks, where the inode table starts, a magic number.

docs.title: Finding inode number i
docs.text:
block  = (i * sizeof(inode)) / blockSize
sector = ((block * blockSize) + inodeStartAddr) / sectorSize
Because every inode is the same size and they sit in one table, finding inode i is simple arithmetic: (start of table) + i × (size of one inode).

Example: inodes are 256 bytes each and the inode table starts 12 KB into the disk. Inode 32 is 32 × 256 = 8 KB into the table, so it's at 12 + 8 = 20 KB from the start of the disk. Disks work in 512-byte sectors, so that's sector 20 × 1024 ÷ 512 = 40.

docs.title: The multi-level index
docs.text:
How does an inode record which blocks hold the file's data? With pointers (block numbers):

  • Direct pointers: the inode itself holds, say, 12 block numbers. 12 × 4 KB = enough for files up to 48 KB.
  • Single indirect pointer: for bigger files, one more pointer leads to a whole block that is full of pointers. A 4 KB block holds 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024 pointers, which adds 1024 × 4 KB = 4 MB.
  • Double indirect: a block of pointers to blocks of pointers: 1024 × 1024 more blocks, about 4 GB. Triple indirect: about 4 TB.

It's lopsided on purpose: most files are small (a typical file is about 2 KB), so they use only the fast direct pointers, while the rare huge files pay for the extra hops.

Other designs: extents store "start at block X, run for N blocks" — compact for files stored contiguously (used by ext4 and XFS). The old FAT file system (USB sticks) links each block to the next like a chain, which makes jumping into the middle of a file slow.

docs.title: Directories
docs.text: A directory is just a special file whose contents are a list of entries. Each entry holds: the inode number, the entry's length, the name's length, and the name. For example (5, 12, 3, "foo"). Every directory also has . (itself) and .. (its parent). Deleting a file just marks its entry empty (inode number 0) so it can be reused. Very large directories may use a search tree instead of a list (XFS uses B-trees).

docs.title: Access paths — count the I/Os
docs.text:
Assume nothing is cached in memory yet. Opening /foo/bar and reading 3 blocks from it:

Step I/Os open: read the root directory's inode (to find its data) → read the root directory's data (find "foo" → its inode number) → read foo's inode → read foo's data (find "bar") → read bar's inode 5 reads Each read(): read bar's inode (where is the block?) → read the data block → write bar's inode back (to update its "last accessed" time) 3 per block

Creating and writing a file costs even more. To create it: find a free inode (read and write the inode bitmap), initialise the new inode, add the name to the directory's data, and update the directory's inode. That's about 10 disk operations. Then for each new block written: find a free block (read and write the data bitmap), write the data, and update the file's inode. That's about 5 operations per block. This is why caching matters so much.

docs.title: Caching & buffering
docs.text:
• Reading: the OS keeps recently used blocks (inodes, directories, file data) in spare RAM, called the page cache. Open the same file again and most or all of those reads come from memory, with no disk access at all.
  • Writing: the OS doesn't write immediately. It waits 5–30 seconds (write buffering) because this lets it:
    • batch — update the bitmap once for many new blocks instead of once each;
    • schedule — send the writes in a good order for the disk;
    • skip some entirely — a temporary file created and deleted within those seconds never reaches the disk.
  • The cost: if the power fails, the last few seconds of writes are lost. Programs that can't accept that (databases) call fsync() to force their data out.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Path lookup walks from the root (inode number usually 2) for every component — long paths cost I/Os.
  • Reads update the access time in the inode → reads cause writes (unless noatime).
  • Bitmaps are per-block, so allocating one block = read + write a bitmap block.
  • Inode size is fixed; number of inodes is fixed at mkfs time in VSFS — you can run out of inodes with free space left.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: draw the layout; compute max file size with 12 direct + 1 indirect; list the 5 reads to open /foo/bar.

Name the five regions of VSFS's on-disk layout.

Superblock, inode bitmap, data bitmap, inode table, data region.

What's in an inode?

Metadata (type, size, owner, permissions, times, link count, block count) and pointers to data blocks.

Max file size with 12 direct pointers, one indirect block, 4 KB blocks, 4-byte pointers?

(12 + 1024) × 4 KB = 4144 KB ≈ 4 MB.

Why does a multi-level (imbalanced) tree make sense for inodes?

Most files are small and fit in direct pointers; the rare large files use indirect blocks.

How many reads to open /foo/bar (no cache)?

Five: root inode, root data, foo inode, foo data, bar inode.

Why does reading a file cause a write?

The inode's last-access time must be updated.

Three benefits of write buffering?

Batching updates into fewer I/Os, better scheduling of writes, and avoiding writes entirely for short-lived files.

Extents vs pointers?

An extent is a start pointer plus a length, describing a contiguous run with little metadata; pointers name each block but are more flexible.

docs.title: L24 · FFS: locality and the Fast File System
docs.text:
Book: Ch 41 (pp. 495–506) · Priority: 🟡 good to know · Time: 25 min · Simulator: file-ffs/ffs.py

In plain words

The first UNIX file system scattered a file's card (inode) and its data all over the disk, so the disk arm kept travelling. It used only about 2% of the disk's speed.

FFS made one simple change: keep things that are used together close together. The disk is split into neighbourhoods (cylinder groups). A file's card and data live in the same neighbourhood, and files in the same folder live near each other. Fewer long arm movements means much faster.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• The old UNIX file system treated the disk like RAM: inodes far from data, free blocks scattered → ~2% of disk bandwidth.
  • FFS made the file system disk-aware: split the disk into cylinder groups (block groups), each with its own superblock copy, bitmaps, inodes and data.
  • Placement policy: keep related things together — a file's inode and data in the same group, files in the same directory together; spread directories across groups. Exception: chunk large files across groups.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we organise file system data structures to improve performance — what allocation policies do we need?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Old UNIX FS: simple, slow → inodes at the front, data at the back = long seeks; free list gets scrambled = fragmentation; 512-byte blocks = small transfers → bigger blocks → ❌ internal fragmentation for small files → 4 KB blocks + 512 B sub-blocks → cylinder groups with local bitmaps/inodes → place related things together → ❌ one big file fills a whole group, hurting locality for everything else → large-file exception: spread chunks across groups, chunk size large enough to amortise seeks. Also: long file names, symlinks, atomic rename.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph G0[Group 0]
        a["S · ib · db · inodes · data"]
    end
    subgraph G1[Group 1]
        b["S · ib · db · inodes · data"]
    end
    subgraph G2[Group 2]
        c["S · ib · db · inodes · data"]
    end
    G0 --- G1 --- G2

docs.title: Placement heuristics
docs.text:
What Where FFS decides where to put new things using a few rules of thumb (heuristics): What Where New directory A group with few directories and plenty of free space, so different directories spread out over the disk New file In the same group as its folder, with its data blocks in the same group as its inode Large file The first 48 KB in the file's own group, then the rest in big chunks spread across other groups, so one huge file doesn't fill up a group that its neighbours need

Why it works: files in the same folder tend to be used together (compiling a project reads all its source files), so keeping them physically close means short arm movements.

docs.title: Amortisation for large files
docs.text: Spreading a big file around costs a seek each time you jump to the next chunk. How big must chunks be for that not to matter? To spend half the time transferring data (50% of the disk's top speed), each transfer must take as long as the seek. With 10 ms of positioning and a 40 MB/s disk, that's 40 MB/s × 10 ms ≈ 409.6 KB per chunk. For 90% of top speed you need ~3.69 MB chunks; for 99%, ~40.6 MB.

docs.title: Other FFS innovations
docs.text:
• Sub-blocks: FFS used bigger 4 KB blocks for speed, but a 1 KB file would waste 3 KB. So small files get 512-byte sub-blocks, which are moved into a full block once the file grows.
  • Skipping blocks: on old, slow systems, by the time the OS asked for the next block, the disk had already spun past it. FFS laid files out on every other block to give the OS time. Modern disks read whole tracks into their own cache, so this trick is obsolete.
  • Usability features that we now take for granted first appeared here: long file names, symbolic links and atomic rename.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• FFS doesn't change the API; it changes placement.
  • Spreading directories ≠ spreading files: files stay near their directory.
  • Large files are deliberately split — the one exception to "keep together".

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: why old UNIX FS was slow (3 reasons); the placement table; the large-file exception.

Why was the original UNIX file system so slow?

It ignored disk geometry: inodes far from data (long seeks), a fragmented free list, and tiny 512-byte blocks.

What is a cylinder (block) group?

A contiguous region of the disk with its own copy of the superblock, inode and data bitmaps, inodes and data blocks.

Where does FFS place a new file and a new directory?

File: same group as its parent directory, with its data near its inode. Directory: a group with few directories and many free inodes.

Why does FFS spread large files across groups?

So one big file doesn't fill a group and destroy locality for other related files; chunks are large enough to amortise the seeks.

What are sub-blocks for?

512-byte allocations for small files to avoid internal fragmentation with 4 KB blocks.

docs.title: L25 · Crash consistency: fsck & journaling
docs.text:
Book: Ch 42 (pp. 507–526) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 55 min · Simulator: file-journaling/fsck.py

In plain words

Saving a file involves several separate disk writes: the data, the file's card (inode) and the free-space checklist (bitmap). If the power dies between them, the disk is left in a muddle, e.g. a card pointing at garbage.

  • fsck: after a crash, inspect the whole disk and fix it. That's like re-checking every shelf in a library, and takes hours on big disks.
  • Journaling: before changing anything, first write a note in a journal ("I'm about to do X, Y, Z"), then a "done writing the note" mark, then do the real writes. After a crash, just replay the finished notes. It works like a shopping list you tick off: even if you're interrupted, you know exactly what's left.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Appending one block needs three writes: inode, data bitmap, data block. A crash between them leaves the disk inconsistent (leaks, garbage, or pointers to freed blocks).
  • fsck scans the whole disk after a crash and repairs metadata — correct-ish but far too slow for big disks.
  • Journaling (write-ahead logging): first write what you're about to do to a log, then commit, then write it in place (checkpoint). On recovery, replay committed transactions. Metadata (ordered) journaling — write data first, journal only metadata — is the common default (ext3/ext4).

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How do we update persistent data structures despite the possibility of a crash or power loss at any moment?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Three writes, crash in between → fsck: check everything on reboot → ❌ time grows with disk size (hours) and it can't know if data is right, only if it's consistent → journaling: write intent to a log first → write TxB + metadata + data + TxE together → ❌ the disk may reorder writes; TxE could land before the data → garbage replayed → write TxB + contents, wait, then write TxE (512 B → atomic) → ❌ data written twice = half bandwidth → metadata journaling: data in place first, then journal metadata → ❌ block reuse bug (deleted directory block reused for a file, replay overwrites it) → revoke records → ordered metadata journaling. Alternatives: soft updates, copy-on-write (ZFS, btrfs, LFS), backpointer-based consistency, optimistic crash consistency.

docs.title: What can go wrong (adding one block to a file)
docs.text:
Adding one block of data to a file needs three separate disk writes:

  1. the data block itself;
  2. the file's inode (to record the new block and the bigger size);
  3. the data bitmap (to mark the block as used).

The disk does them one at a time. Here's what the disk looks like if the power dies after only some of them:

What made it to disk Result Only the data The file system is fine; the new data is simply lost Only the inode The inode points to a block holding old garbage, and the bitmap says that block is free, so it could be given to another file Only the bitmap A block is marked used but nothing uses it: wasted space (a space leak) Inode + bitmap The structures agree, but the file now contains garbage where the new data should be Inode + data The file looks right, but the bitmap says the block is free, so it may be handed out again and overwritten Bitmap + data The block is used but no file points to it: a space leak

docs.title: fsck checks
docs.text:
fsck (file system check) runs after a crash and checks everything for consistency: Does the superblock look sane? Do the bitmaps match what the inodes actually use? Does each file's link count match the number of directory entries pointing to it (this means walking the entire directory tree)? Do two files claim the same block? Does every directory have proper . and .. entries? Files that no directory points to are put in a folder called lost+found.

It works, but it reads the whole disk, which takes hours on a big one. And it can only make things consistent: it can't know whether the data is the right data.

docs.title: Data journaling — the protocol
docs.text:
The idea (called write-ahead logging): before changing anything in place, first write a description of all the changes to a reserved area of the disk, the journal. A group of changes that belong together is a transaction. It's marked with a begin block (TxB) and an end block (TxE, the "commit").

sequenceDiagram
    participant FS
    participant J as Journal
    participant D as Final locations
    FS->>J: 1. Journal write: TxB, inode, bitmap, data
    Note over FS,J: wait for completion
    FS->>J: 2. Journal commit: TxE (one 512-B sector → atomic)
    Note over FS,J: transaction is now committed
    FS->>D: 3. Checkpoint: write inode, bitmap, data in place
    FS->>J: 4. Free: mark transaction free in journal superblock

Why the waits matter: the disk may reorder writes for speed. If TxE were sent together with the rest, it could reach the disk before the data it vouches for. A crash at that moment would leave a "complete-looking" transaction full of garbage. So: write everything else, wait until it's on disk, then write TxE. TxE fits in one 512-byte sector, and single-sector writes are all-or-nothing, so the commit either happened or it didn't.

Recovery after a crash: read the journal. Every transaction that has its TxE is complete, so replay it (write its blocks to their real places again). Transactions without a TxE never committed, so ignore them; the real data was never touched. Replaying a transaction twice does no harm, since it writes the same blocks with the same contents.

Batching: the OS doesn't journal every tiny change separately. It gathers many updates into one big transaction in memory and writes it every few seconds.

The journal has a fixed size: once a transaction has been checkpointed, its space can be reused. The journal is used round and round like a ring (circular buffer), and a small header (the journal superblock) records which transactions are still pending.

docs.title: Metadata (ordered) journaling
docs.text:
Data journaling writes every data block twice (once in the journal, once in place), which halves write speed. Most systems instead journal only the metadata (inodes, bitmaps: the file system's own bookkeeping) and write the user's data straight to its final place, but first:

1. Data write:      write data to final location         (wait)*
2. Journal write:   TxB + metadata (inode, bitmap)       (wait)
3. Journal commit:  TxE                                  (wait)
4. Checkpoint:      write metadata in place
5. Free
*Steps 1 and 2 can be sent together, but both must finish before step 3.

Why write the data first? If the inode (which points to the data block) committed first and the crash came before the data was written, the file would point at garbage. The general rule: write the thing being pointed to before the thing that points to it.

  • Writeback mode (no ordering at all) is faster but allows exactly that garbage-pointing case.
  • Revoke records: a subtle case where a block is freed and reused for something else. A revoke entry in the journal tells recovery "don't replay the old version of this block".
  • Speed trick (ext4): store a checksum of the transaction in TxE, so everything can be written in one go without waiting. If the checksum doesn't match at recovery, the transaction is treated as incomplete.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Approach Recovery time Normal-path cost Notes fsck Grows with disk size — hours None Only fixes the structures, not the data Data journaling Grows only with journal size — seconds All data written twice Strongest guarantee Ordered metadata journaling Seconds Only metadata written twice The default in Linux ext3/ext4 Copy-on-write (ZFS, btrfs, LFS) Fast Never overwrites anything in place, so there's nothing half-changed to fix See L26 Soft updates Fast Orders every write very carefully so the disk is always consistent Very complex to implement

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Journaling guarantees consistency, not that your last writes survive. Use fsync.
  • TxE must be written after the rest of the transaction completes (or use checksums).
  • In ordered mode, data goes before the journal commit — not after.
  • fsck is "consistent" not "correct": it can't tell whether the data in a block is the right data.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the six crash scenarios (at least four); the data-journaling 4 steps; metadata-journaling 5 steps with the ordering rule.

Which three blocks must be written to append one data block?

The inode, the data bitmap, and the data block.

What's the main drawback of fsck?

It scans the entire disk, so recovery takes time proportional to disk size — far too slow for large disks.

List the steps of data journaling.

Journal write (TxB + contents), journal commit (TxE), checkpoint (write in place), free the journal space.

Why must TxE be written separately, after the rest?

The disk can reorder writes; if TxE lands first and the crash hits, recovery could replay garbage. TxE fits in one sector, so its write is atomic.

What does recovery do with the journal?

Replays (redoes) every committed transaction — those with a TxE — and ignores incomplete ones.

In ordered metadata journaling, when is user data written?

To its final location before the journal commit, so metadata never points to garbage.

What rule underlies crash-consistent write ordering?

Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it.

Why do metadata journaling instead of data journaling?

Data journaling writes all data twice, halving write bandwidth; metadata is small.

docs.title: L26 · Log-structured file systems & data integrity
docs.text:
Book: Ch 43 (pp. 527–542) 🟡 · Ch 44 (pp. 543–554) 🟡 · Time: 40 min · Simulators: file-lfs/lfs.py, file-integrity/checksum.py

In plain words

LFS treats the disk like a diary. You never go back and edit old pages; every change is written on the next blank pages, in one sweep. Writing is very fast because it's all sequential. The cost: you need an index of where the latest version of each thing is (the inode map), and someone must occasionally clear out pages full of outdated entries (the cleaner).

Data integrity: disks sometimes fail quietly, returning wrong data with no error. A checksum is a fingerprint stored with the data. Recompute it when you read, and if the fingerprints don't match, the data is corrupt and you use a backup copy.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• LFS: memory is big, so reads hit the cache — optimise for writes. Buffer all updates (data and inodes) into a big segment and write it sequentially to free space. Never overwrite in place.
  • Inodes now move, so an inode map (imap) finds them; pieces of the imap are written with each segment and located through the fixed checkpoint region. Old versions become garbage → a cleaner compacts segments.
  • Data integrity: disks also fail partially — latent sector errors (detectable) and silent corruption (not). Use checksums stored separately, plus block address and write verification to catch misdirected and lost writes; scrub periodically.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: LFS: how can a file system turn all writes into sequential writes? · Integrity: how do we make sure the data we read back is the data we wrote?

docs.title: The story chain (LFS)
docs.text: Memory grows → most reads hit cache; disk transfer improves faster than seek → write everything sequentially → ❌ one small write at a time still pays rotation → buffer into large segments (MBs) → ❌ inodes are no longer at fixed places → imap: inum → inode address → ❌ where is the imap? → write imap chunks in the log too; fixed checkpoint region points to the latest chunks → ❌ old copies pile up → cleaner: read M segments, write live blocks into N < M new ones → ❌ which blocks are live? → segment summary block: (inum, offset) per block; check if the inode still points here → ❌ crash while writing the CR → two CRs, alternate, with timestamps.

docs.title: Writing in LFS
docs.text:
The LFS rule: never overwrite anything. Every change — new data, the updated inode, everything — is collected in memory and then written together as one big sequential chunk, a segment (several MB), onto free space. Large sequential writes are what disks do fastest (L20).

That creates a puzzle. A normal file system keeps inode 7 in a fixed spot, but in LFS a new copy of inode 7 is written somewhere new every time the file changes. So how do you find the latest inode 7? With an inode map (imap): a table "inode 7 is currently at disk address X". Pieces of the imap are written into the log too, and one fixed place on the disk, the checkpoint region, says where the latest imap pieces are.

docs.title: Reading a file in LFS
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CR["Checkpoint region<br/>(fixed location)"] --> IM["imap chunk<br/>(latest in log)"]
    IM --> IN["inode k<br/>(somewhere in the log)"]
    IN --> DB["data blocks<br/>(in the log)"]

Follow the arrows: fixed checkpoint region → latest imap → the file's latest inode → its data. In practice the imap is kept in memory, so reading costs about the same as in a normal file system.

docs.title: Write cost amortisation
docs.text:
How big should a segment be? Each segment write pays one seek + rotation first, so the segment must be big enough to make that cost small. To get a fraction F of the disk's top speed: D = F/(1−F) × Rpeak × Tposition.

Example: 10 ms positioning, 100 MB/s top speed, and we want 90%. F/(1−F) = 0.9/0.1 = 9, so D = 9 × 100 MB/s × 0.01 s = 9 MB per segment.

docs.title: Garbage collection
docs.text:
Because nothing is overwritten, old versions pile up and the disk fills with outdated blocks (garbage). A background cleaner reads a few old segments, copies out only the blocks that are still current (live), packs them into a fresh segment, and frees the old ones.

  • How does it know a block is live? Each segment starts with a summary block noting, for every block, "this was block #3 of inode 7". The cleaner looks up inode 7's current version: if it still points at this exact address, the block is live; otherwise it's an outdated copy.
  • Which segments to clean first? Segments full of frequently changing (hot) data: wait, because more of their blocks will become garbage soon anyway. Segments of rarely changing (cold) data: clean sooner.
  • Why moving inodes doesn't ripple upward: directories store a file's inode number, not its disk address. When an inode moves, only the imap changes; the directory doesn't need rewriting.

docs.title: Crash recovery
docs.text:
The checkpoint region is updated every ~30 seconds. LFS keeps two of them and alternates between them, with a timestamp at both the start and the end of each. If the power fails while one is being written, its two timestamps won't match, so LFS uses the other, older one. Then it reads forward through any segments written after that checkpoint (roll forward) to recover recent work.

LFS ideas live on in copy-on-write file systems (WAFL/NetApp, ZFS, btrfs) and in SSD FTLs.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detected? Example cause Disks don't only fail completely. They also fail partially: the disk mostly works, but some blocks go bad. Failure Does the disk notice? Example cause Latent sector error (LSE) — a block can't be read Yes: the disk's internal error-correcting code (ECC) fails, and the read returns an error Scratched surface, cosmic rays Silent corruption — a block reads back wrong No: you get wrong data with no error Buggy disk firmware, faulty cable Misdirected write No The right data was written to the wrong block Lost write No The disk said "done" but never actually wrote

docs.title: Handling them
docs.text:
• Unreadable blocks (LSEs): the disk reports them, so just rebuild the block from a mirror or parity (RAID). The danger is a second bad block turning up while rebuilding a failed disk, which is why some systems keep extra parity (e.g. NetApp's RAID-DP).
  • Silent corruption → checksums. A checksum is a small "fingerprint" computed from a block's contents (simple ones: XOR, Fletcher; stronger: CRC). Store it separately from the block. On every read, recompute the fingerprint; if it doesn't match the stored one, the block is corrupt, so use a redundant copy instead.
  • Misdirected writes: store the block's own address next to its checksum. If you read block 50 and the record says "I am block 70", something was written to the wrong place.
  • Lost writes: either read every block back right after writing it (write verify — reliable but slow), or keep a second copy of the checksum elsewhere, e.g. in the inode (ZFS does this). A lost write then leaves a mismatch.
  • Scrubbing: checksums only help when you read the data. So the system periodically reads every block in the background to catch damage before you need the data.
  • Costs: a little space (8 bytes per 4 KB block ≈ 0.2%) and a little CPU time to compute fingerprints.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• LFS writes inodes into the log too — not only data.
  • The checkpoint region is the only fixed structure, and it's updated rarely (every ~30 s).
  • A checksum can't fix data by itself — it only detects; recovery needs redundancy.
  • Checksums alone can't catch misdirected or lost writes (the wrong block has a valid checksum for itself).

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the LFS chain; CR → imap → inode → data; the cleaner's liveness test; the four failure types with their fix.

What's the core idea of LFS?

Buffer all updates (data and metadata) in memory and write them sequentially as large segments to free space; never overwrite in place.

Why does LFS need an inode map?

Inodes move every time they're written, so the imap records each inode's current location.

How does LFS find the imap?

Through the checkpoint region, a fixed location that points to the latest imap pieces; it's updated periodically.

How does the LFS cleaner decide if a block is live?

The segment summary block gives the block's inode number and offset; if that inode (via the imap) still points to this address, it's live.

What is a latent sector error vs silent corruption?

LSE: the disk detects the bad sector and returns an error. Silent corruption: the disk returns wrong data with no error.

How do you detect misdirected writes?

Store the disk and sector address alongside the checksum and verify it on read.

What is disk scrubbing?

Periodically reading all blocks and verifying checksums to find corruption early.

docs.title: One-page cheat sheet
docs.text:
Use it as a test first

Before reading, take a blank page and try to write this sheet from memory. Then compare.

This page is deliberately compressed — it's for revision after the lessons, not for first learning. If a line doesn't make sense, follow it back to its lesson, or hover over the underlined words for a quick definition.

docs.title: Virtualization — CPU
docs.text:
• Process = address space + registers (PC, SP) + open files. States: Running ⇄ Ready, Running → Blocked → Ready.
  • fork() → 0 in child, child PID in parent. exec() replaces the program, returns only on error. wait() blocks until a child exits.
  • LDE: user mode + trap for syscalls (trap table set at boot) + timer interrupt to regain control. Context switch: HW saves user regs → kernel stack; OS saves kernel regs → PCB.
  • Turnaround = completion − arrival · Response = first run − arrival.
  • FIFO (convoy) → SJF → STCF (optimal turnaround) → RR (good response, bad turnaround).
  • MLFQ rules: (1) higher priority runs (2) equal → RR (3) new jobs at top (4) used up allotment at a level → move down (5) every S, boost all to top.
  • Lottery: share ≈ tickets. Stride: run lowest pass, pass += stride. Multi-CPU: cache affinity; SQMS vs MQMS + work stealing.

docs.title: Virtualization — Memory
docs.text:
• Address space: code · heap ↓ · … · ↑ stack. Goals: transparency, efficiency, protection.
  • Base/bounds: PA = VA + base, fault if VA ≥ bounds. Segmentation: per-segment base/bounds; top bits pick the segment; stack grows negative → external fragmentation.
  • Free space: split, coalesce, header; best/worst/first/next fit; slab; buddy (internal frag).
  • Paging: VA = VPN | offset; PT[VPN] → PFN; PA = PFN | offset. PTE bits: valid, prot, present, dirty, reference.
  • 32-bit, 4 KB pages, 4-byte PTE → 2²⁰ PTEs = 4 MB per process. 4 KB page / 4 B = 1024 PTEs per page → 10 bits per level.
  • TLB: cache of VPN→PFN; locality; HW-managed (x86) vs SW-managed (MIPS, retry instruction); flush vs ASID. Coverage = entries × page size.
  • Multi-level PT: page directory → pages of PTEs; unused regions cost nothing; +1 memory access per level on TLB miss. Inverted PT: one entry per physical frame.
  • Swapping: present bit; page fault → OS reads from swap, retries. AMAT = T_M + P_miss × T_D.
  • Policies: OPT (furthest future) · FIFO (Belady's anomaly) · Random · LRU · Clock (use bit). Looping over N+1 pages kills LRU/FIFO. Thrashing → admission control / OOM killer. Copy-on-write, demand zeroing.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
• Threads share address space; each has its own registers + stack. x++ = load, add, store → race.
  • Critical section · race condition · indeterminate · mutual exclusion · atomic.
  • Lock criteria: correctness, fairness, performance. Primitives: test-and-set, compare-and-swap, LL/SC, fetch-and-add (→ ticket lock, fair). Spin bad on 1 CPU → yield → queues + park/unpark (setpark), futex, two-phase locks.
  • Sloppy counter (per-CPU, threshold S); hash table with per-bucket locks; queue with head+tail locks.
  • CV: wait(c, m) releases m and sleeps atomically. Hold the lock. Use while. Producer/consumer: two CVs (empty, fill). Broadcast = covering condition.
  • Semaphore: wait = dec, sleep if < 0; post = inc, wake one. Init 1 = lock, 0 = ordering, N = resources. P/C: empty=MAX, full=0, mutex=1 — mutex inside. RW lock (writers starve). Philosophers: one picks forks in reverse.
  • Non-deadlock bugs: atomicity and order violations (97%).
  • Deadlock = mutual exclusion + hold-and-wait + no preemption + circular wait. Fix: lock ordering; trylock (livelock); lock-free CAS.
  • Event loop: select/poll, no locks on 1 CPU, never block → async I/O, continuations.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
• Device: status/command/data registers. Polling (fast devices) vs interrupts (slow); hybrid, coalescing; DMA. I/O instructions vs memory-mapped I/O.
  • T_I/O = seek + rotation + transfer. Avg rotation = ½ rotation (15K RPM → 2 ms). Random 4 KB ≈ 6–13 ms → ~0.3–0.7 MB/s; sequential ≈ 100+ MB/s. Only 512-B sector writes atomic.
  • Disk scheduling: SSTF (starves) → SCAN / C-SCAN → SPTF (in drive).
  • RAID: 0 stripe · 1 mirror · 4 parity disk (small writes R/2) · 5 rotated parity (N/4·R). Small parity write = 4 I/Os: P_new = (C_old ⊕ C_new) ⊕ P_old. Capacity: N·B, N·B/2, (N−1)·B.
  • File = bytes + inode number; directory = (name, inum). fd → open file table (offset) → inode. fsync to persist. rename is atomic. Hard link = same inode (refcount); symlink = path, can dangle.
  • VSFS: superblock · inode bitmap · data bitmap · inodes · data. 12 direct + indirect (1024 ptrs) + double + triple. Open /foo/bar = 5 reads. Page cache + write buffering (5–30 s).
  • FFS: cylinder groups; file near its directory, data near its inode; spread directories; large-file exception.
  • Crash: inode + bitmap + data. fsck = slow full scan. Journaling: TxB+contents → wait → TxE (commit) → checkpoint → free. Replay committed. Ordered metadata journaling: data first, then journal metadata. Pointed-to before pointer.
  • LFS: buffer into segments, write sequentially; imap via checkpoint region; cleaner + segment summary. Integrity: LSE vs silent corruption, checksums stored separately, block address for misdirected writes, write verify for lost writes, scrubbing.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
• Reliability = ack + timeout + retry + sequence numbers. RPC stubs marshal. End-to-end argument.
  • NFSv2: stateless, file handle (volume, inode, generation), idempotent ops → retry. Flush on close, GETATTR (+3 s attr cache). Server commits before replying.
  • AFS: whole-file caching on local disk, callbacks, FIDs → scales; last closer wins.

docs.title: The numbers to know cold
docs.text: Number Value Page size 4 KB → 12-bit offset PTEs per 4 KB page (4 B each) 1024 → 10 bits/level Linear PT, 32-bit 4 MB per process TLB size 32–128 entries; hit ~1 cycle Context switch / syscall ~µs (sub-µs modern) Timer interrupt every few ms (~10 ms) Memory access ~100 ns Random disk I/O ~5–15 ms Sequential disk ~100–200 MB/s Disk sector 512 B (atomic write unit) Write buffering delay 5–30 s

docs.title: Mixed recall drills
docs.text: These questions are interleaved on purpose: each round jumps between parts, the way exams and interviews do. Answer out loud or on paper before opening the answer. Mark the ones you miss and redo them in 3 days.

docs.title: Round 1 — warm-up (one-liners)
docs.text:
1. A process calls fork() and then the child calls exec("ls"). How many processes exist and what does each run?

Two: the parent continues its own code; the child (same PID as after fork) now runs ls.

2. What's the minimum number of disk I/Os to read the first block of /a/b (cold cache)?

Root inode, root data, a's inode, a's data, b's inode, b's data block = 6 reads (plus possibly an atime write).

3. Which MLFQ rule fixes starvation?

Rule 5: boost all jobs to the top queue every S time units.

4. Semaphore initialised to 0: lock or ordering?

Ordering — the first wait blocks until someone posts.

5. What's the average rotational delay of a 10,000 RPM disk?

One rotation = 6 ms → average 3 ms.

6. A TLB has 64 entries and pages are 4 KB. What's its coverage?

256 KB.

7. What does RAID-5 cost for one small random write?

4 I/Os: read old data, read old parity, write new data, write new parity.

8. Why must pthread_cond_wait be inside a while loop?

Mesa semantics / spurious wakeups — the condition might not hold when the thread runs.

docs.title: Round 2 — "why not just…?"
docs.text:
9. Why not just let user programs disable interrupts to make critical sections atomic?

A program could disable them and never re-enable (taking over the machine); it doesn't work on multiprocessors; interrupts can be lost.

10. Why not just use one huge page size (say 1 MB) to shrink page tables?

Internal fragmentation: small processes waste most of each page. (Huge pages are used selectively, e.g. for databases, to boost TLB coverage.)

11. Why not just run fsck after every crash?

It scans the whole disk; on large disks recovery takes hours, and it only restores consistency, not correctness.

12. Why not just use FIFO page replacement — it's simple?

It ignores how often or recently a page is used (evicts hot pages) and suffers Belady's anomaly.

13. Why not just spin while waiting for a lock?

On one CPU, the holder can't run while you spin, so you waste a whole slice; with many threads, CPU is burnt for nothing. Fine only for very short critical sections on multicores.

14. Why not just keep NFS servers stateful to make caching easier?

Crash recovery becomes hard: the server would have to rebuild who has what open/cached. Stateless + idempotent means clients simply retry.

15. Why not just use SSTF for disk scheduling?

Starvation of far-away requests, and it ignores rotation time.

16. Why not just put a lock around the whole hash table?

It serializes all operations; per-bucket locks let unrelated operations run in parallel and scale far better.

docs.title: Round 3 — connect two parts
docs.text:
17. How are a TLB and a file system's page cache alike?

Both cache the result of an expensive lookup (page table walk / disk read) and rely on locality; both need a replacement policy and have consistency issues (TLB on context switch, page cache on crash).

18. Where does the idea "write the pointed-to object before the pointer" appear?

Ordered journaling (data before metadata commit), soft updates, and safe list insertion in concurrent code (initialise the node before linking it).

19. What do multi-level page tables and inode indirect blocks have in common?

Both are imbalanced trees of indirection that allocate only the parts actually used — optimising for sparse/small cases.

20. SJF appears in two places in the book. Where, and what's the shared weakness?

CPU scheduling (SJF/STCF) and disk scheduling (SSTF). Both can starve long/far jobs.

21. LFS and SSD flash translation layers share one key idea. What is it?

Never overwrite in place: write to fresh locations log-style, keep a mapping, and garbage-collect old versions.

22. Why does a context switch hurt performance beyond the cost of saving registers?

Cold caches and a stale TLB (flushed or with other ASIDs' entries), so the next process takes misses.

23. How does copy-on-write make fork()+exec() cheap?

fork shares pages read-only instead of copying them; exec then replaces the address space, so most pages are never copied.

24. What's the deadlock-prevention idea behind the dining philosophers fix, and where else is it used?

Break circular wait by imposing an order on lock acquisition — the same as lock ordering by address in kernel code.

docs.title: Round 4 — calculate
docs.text:
25. 16-bit address space, 1 KB pages. How many bits of VPN and offset? How many PTEs?

Offset 10 bits, VPN 6 bits, 64 PTEs.

26. Jobs A=10, B=20, C=30 arrive at t=0. Average turnaround under SJF?

Completions 10, 30, 60 → (10+30+60)/3 = 33.3.

27. 48-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages, 8-byte PTEs. How many levels of page table?

36 VPN bits; 512 PTEs per page = 9 bits per level → 4 levels.

28. Memory 100 ns, disk 10 ms, 0.1% of accesses page-fault. AMAT?

100 ns + 0.001 × 10 ms = 100 ns + 10 µs ≈ 10.1 µs.

29. RAID-5 with 5 disks of 1 TB. Usable capacity, and random write throughput if each disk does R MB/s?

4 TB; random writes ≈ (5/4)·R.

30. Inode with 12 direct pointers and one double-indirect block (no single indirect). 4 KB blocks, 4-byte pointers. Max file size?

(12 + 1024²) × 4 KB = 48 KB + 4 GB ≈ 4 GB.
