docs.title: Virtualization
docs.text:
L01 · Intro & the three pieces

Question Answer What are the "three easy pieces"? Virtualization, concurrency, persistence. Why can two processes print the same address for a variable yet hold different values? Each has its own virtual address space; the same virtual address maps to different physical memory. Why does a shared counter incremented by two threads end up wrong? counter++ is load–add–store. If a context switch hits between them, one thread's update overwrites the other's. The three instructions are not atomic. How does a system call differ from a procedure call? It traps into the kernel and raises the hardware privilege level, so the OS can perform restricted operations; a procedure call stays in user mode.

L02 · Processes & fork / exec / wait

Question Answer What does fork() return in the parent and in the child? Child's PID in the parent; 0 in the child; −1 on failure. When does exec() return? Only if it fails. On success the calling program is replaced and the old code is gone. Why does UNIX split process creation into fork() and exec()? So code can run in the child between the two, to set up redirection, pipes or other environment changes before the new program starts. What are the three main process states and their transitions? Running, Ready, Blocked. Running→Ready (descheduled), Ready→Running (scheduled), Running→Blocked (I/O starts), Blocked→Ready (I/O done). What is a zombie process? One that has exited but whose parent hasn't called wait() to collect its exit status. What does the OS store in a process control block (PCB)? Saved registers (context), state, PID, parent, memory info, open files, and similar per-process data.

L03 · Limited direct execution

Question Answer What does "limited direct execution" mean? Run the program directly on the CPU for speed, but limit it: user mode, traps for privileged operations, and a timer interrupt so the OS regains control. What is the trap table and when is it set up? A table of handler addresses for traps/interrupts. The kernel installs it at boot using a privileged instruction. Why does the cooperative approach fail? A process stuck in an infinite loop never makes a syscall, so the OS never runs again; you must reboot. How does the OS regain control in the non-cooperative approach? A hardware timer interrupt every few milliseconds jumps into the OS's interrupt handler. In a context switch, which registers does the hardware save and which does the OS save? Hardware saves the user registers onto the process's kernel stack on the interrupt. The OS saves the kernel registers into the process's PCB in switch(). Why pass a system-call number instead of an address? So user code can only reach approved kernel entry points; it can't jump into the middle of the kernel.

L04 · Scheduling basics: FIFO, SJF, STCF, RR

Question Answer Define turnaround time and response time. Turnaround = completion − arrival. Response = first run − arrival. What is the convoy effect? Short jobs stuck waiting behind a long job in FIFO, inflating average turnaround. What's the difference between SJF and STCF? SJF is non-preemptive: it picks the shortest job when choosing. STCF preempts the running job whenever a new job has less remaining time. Why does RR have poor turnaround? It stretches every job out across many slices, so all jobs finish near the end. What's the trade-off in choosing RR's time slice? Shorter = better response but more context-switch overhead; longer amortizes the switch cost but hurts response. How does the scheduler use I/O to improve utilisation? When a job blocks on I/O, run another job; treat each CPU burst as a separate job so interactive bursts run quickly and overlap with I/O.

L05 · MLFQ, lottery & multiprocessor scheduling

Question Answer What is MLFQ's key idea? Use several priority queues and adjust a job's priority based on its observed behaviour, so it approximates SJF without knowing job lengths. Which MLFQ rule prevents starvation, and what else does it fix? Rule 5 (periodic priority boost). It also lets a job that became interactive get back to high priority. How could a program game the original MLFQ, and what fixes it? Issue an I/O just before its slice ends to stay at high priority. Fixed by accounting for total time used at a level (new Rule 4). Why do higher MLFQ queues get shorter time slices? They hold interactive jobs that need fast switching; lower queues hold CPU-bound jobs that benefit from long slices with less switching. Lottery vs stride scheduling? Lottery picks a random ticket each slice — simple, no global state, fair on average. Stride is deterministic (run lowest pass, add stride) — exactly fair but needs global state. How does Linux CFS pick the next process? The one with the lowest virtual runtime, stored in a red-black tree; nice values weight how fast vruntime grows. Single-queue vs multi-queue multiprocessor scheduling? Single-queue: simple, balanced, but lock contention and poor cache affinity. Multi-queue: scalable and affinity-friendly, but needs migration/work stealing to fix load imbalance.

L06 · Address spaces & the memory API

Question Answer What are the three segments of a typical address space and how do they grow? Code (fixed), heap (grows towards higher addresses), stack (grows towards lower addresses). What are the three goals of virtual memory? Transparency, efficiency (time and space), protection/isolation. Is malloc() a system call? No. It's a library routine; it gets memory from the OS with brk/sbrk or mmap. Why must you allocate strlen(s)+1 bytes to copy a string? To leave room for the terminating null byte. What is a dangling pointer? A pointer to memory that has already been freed; using it is undefined behaviour.

L07 · Address translation: base/bounds & segmentation

Question Answer How does base-and-bounds translation work? Physical = virtual + base; if virtual ≥ bounds, the hardware raises an exception. Where do base and bounds live, and who can change them? In the CPU's MMU; only privileged (kernel-mode) instructions can change them. The OS saves/restores them in the PCB on a context switch. What problem does segmentation solve over base-and-bounds? It avoids wasting physical memory for the unused space between heap and stack, by relocating each segment separately. How does the hardware know which segment a virtual address is in? Typically the top bits of the virtual address select the segment; the rest is the offset. What is external fragmentation and why does segmentation cause it? Free memory split into many small variable-sized holes. Segments have different sizes, so allocating and freeing them leaves gaps too small to use. How are code segments shared between processes? With protection bits: a read-execute-only code segment can be mapped into many address spaces safely.

L08 · Free-space management

Question Answer How does free() know the size of the block? It reads a header stored just before the returned pointer, which holds the size (and a magic number for integrity). What is coalescing? Merging a freed chunk with adjacent free chunks into a single larger free chunk. Best fit vs first fit? Best fit searches the whole list for the smallest hole that fits (less waste, slow, slivers). First fit takes the first hole that fits (fast, slivers at the list head). How does the buddy allocator make coalescing easy? Blocks are powers of two; a block's buddy address differs by a single bit, so checking and merging is quick and recursive. What's the main downside of the buddy allocator? Internal fragmentation, because requests are rounded up to a power of two.

L09 · Paging

Question Answer What is a page vs a page frame? A page is a fixed-size chunk of virtual memory; a page frame is the same-size slot in physical memory. How is a virtual address split under paging? High bits = virtual page number (VPN); low log2(page size) bits = offset. Which part of the address does the page table translate? Only the VPN → PFN. The offset is copied unchanged. How large is a linear page table for a 32-bit space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte PTEs? 2^20 entries × 4 bytes = 4 MB per process. Why is basic paging slow? Each memory reference needs an extra memory access to fetch the PTE first. Valid bit vs present bit? Valid: the page belongs to the address space. Present: the page is currently in physical memory (not swapped out). Two advantages of paging over segmentation? No external fragmentation (all frames same size), and flexible support for sparse address spaces.

L10 · TLBs: making paging fast

Question Answer What does the TLB store? Recently used virtual-to-physical page translations (VPN → PFN plus protection and other bits). Why does the TLB work well for most programs? Spatial and temporal locality: nearby accesses fall in the same page and pages get reused. Hardware-managed vs software-managed TLB miss? Hardware: the CPU walks the page table itself (x86). Software: the CPU traps to the OS, which walks the table and installs the entry (MIPS) — more flexible. What's special about returning from a TLB-miss trap? It must retry the instruction that caused the miss, unlike a syscall return which continues with the next instruction. How do ASIDs help with context switches? Entries are tagged with the address-space ID, so the TLB can hold translations for several processes without flushing. What is TLB coverage? Number of entries × page size — the amount of memory reachable without a TLB miss.

L11 · Smaller page tables: multi-level & friends

Question Answer Why are linear page tables wasteful? They allocate a PTE for every virtual page, even the vast unused region between heap and stack. How does a multi-level page table save space? The page table is split into page-sized chunks; a page directory tracks them, and chunks with no valid entries are never allocated. What's the cost of a two-level page table? On a TLB miss, two memory accesses instead of one to translate (plus more complexity). How many 4-byte PTEs fit in a 4 KB page, and what does that imply? 1024 → each level indexes with 10 bits. What's an inverted page table? A single system-wide table with one entry per physical frame, recording which process and virtual page use it; searched with a hash table. Why not just use bigger pages? Internal fragmentation: most of each big page goes unused for small allocations.

L12 · Swapping: going beyond physical memory

Question Answer What is the present bit? A PTE bit saying whether the page is in physical memory (1) or swapped out to disk (0). What happens on a page fault? The OS finds a free frame (evicting one if needed), reads the page from swap, sets present=1 and the PFN, and the faulting instruction is retried. The process is blocked during the I/O. Write the average memory access time formula. AMAT = T_M + P_miss × T_D. What does OPT evict and why can't we use it? The page that will be used furthest in the future; it requires knowing the future. What is Belady's anomaly? With FIFO, increasing cache size can increase the number of misses. LRU and OPT (stack algorithms) don't have it. How does the Clock algorithm work? Pages in a circle with a hardware-set use bit. The hand sweeps: use bit 1 → clear it and move on; use bit 0 → evict. Which workload makes LRU and FIFO miss every time? Looping sequentially over one more page than the cache holds. What is thrashing and how is it handled? Memory is oversubscribed so the system spends its time paging. Run fewer processes (admission control) or kill one (OOM killer). What is copy-on-write? After fork, parent and child share pages read-only; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
L13 · Threads & race conditions

Question Answer What do threads in a process share, and what is private to each? Shared: code, heap, globals, open files (the address space). Private: registers, program counter, stack. Why might counter++ give the wrong result with two threads? It's load, add, store; an interrupt between them lets the other thread read the old value, and one update is lost. Define critical section, race condition and mutual exclusion. Critical section: code touching shared data. Race condition: result depends on timing. Mutual exclusion: only one thread in the critical section at a time. Two reasons to use threads? Parallelism on multiple CPUs, and avoiding blocking the program on slow I/O. Why is returning a pointer to a local variable from a thread a bug? The local lives on the thread's stack, which is freed when the thread exits.

L14 · Locks

Question Answer Three criteria for evaluating a lock? Correctness (mutual exclusion), fairness (no starvation), performance (overhead uncontended, one CPU, many CPUs). Why doesn't disabling interrupts work as a general lock? It's privileged (programs could abuse it), doesn't work on multiprocessors, can lose interrupts, and is slow on modern CPUs. OK only inside the kernel briefly. Why does a simple flag-based lock fail? Testing the flag and setting it are separate steps; an interrupt in between lets two threads both see it free and both enter. What does test-and-set do? Atomically returns the old value at an address and sets it to a new value. How does a ticket lock guarantee fairness? Fetch-and-add hands out increasing tickets; the lock serves turns in order, so each thread gets in once its number comes up. Why are spin locks bad on a single CPU? A waiting thread spins for its whole time slice, but the holder can't run to release the lock during that time. What is the wakeup/waiting race and how is it fixed? A thread about to park() gets unparked before it sleeps, then sleeps forever. Solaris fixes it with setpark(); futexes check the value atomically in the kernel. What is a two-phase lock? Spin for a short time hoping the lock frees up soon; if not, sleep until woken.

L15 · Lock-based concurrent data structures

Question Answer How does a sloppy (approximate) counter work? Per-CPU local counters with their own locks; when one reaches threshold S it's added to the global counter. Low contention, but the global value lags. What's the effect of increasing S in a sloppy counter? Better scalability, less accurate global count. Why does the Michael & Scott queue use a dummy node? To keep the head and tail operations on separate nodes so the head lock and tail lock can be held concurrently. Why does a hash table with per-bucket locks scale well? Operations on different buckets don't contend for the same lock. What's hand-over-hand locking and why is it often slow? A lock per node; you grab the next node's lock before releasing the current one. The per-node lock overhead usually outweighs the extra concurrency.

L16 · Condition variables

Question Answer What does pthread_cond_wait(c, m) do? Atomically releases mutex m and puts the thread to sleep on c; when woken, re-acquires m before returning. Why must you re-check the condition in a while loop? Mesa semantics: the signal is only a hint and the state may change before the woken thread runs; spurious wakeups can also happen. Why do we need a state variable along with a CV? CVs have no memory. If signal happens before wait, it's lost; the state variable records that the condition already holds. Why does producer/consumer need two condition variables? So a consumer only wakes producers and a producer only wakes consumers; with one CV a consumer can wake another consumer and everyone sleeps. What is a covering condition? Using broadcast to wake all waiters when you can't tell which one should proceed; each re-checks its condition. Mesa vs Hoare semantics? Mesa: signal is a hint; the woken thread runs later and must re-check. Hoare: the woken thread runs immediately with the guarantee. Real systems use Mesa.

L17 · Semaphores

Question Answer What do sem_wait and sem_post do? sem_wait decrements and sleeps if the value is negative; sem_post increments and wakes one waiter if any. Both are atomic. What does a negative semaphore value mean? Its magnitude is the number of threads waiting. What initial value makes a semaphore a lock? For ordering? 1 for a lock (binary semaphore); 0 for ordering (wait until another thread posts). Why must the mutex be acquired inside wait(empty)/wait(full) in producer/consumer? Otherwise a thread can sleep on full/empty while holding the mutex, so the other side can never get the mutex to post — deadlock. How does a reader-writer lock work and what's its weakness? The first reader takes the write lock, the last reader releases it; writers need the write lock. Readers can starve writers. How do you avoid deadlock in dining philosophers? Make one philosopher acquire forks in the opposite order, breaking the circular wait. Key difference between a semaphore and a condition variable? A semaphore has state (its count), so a post before a wait isn't lost; a CV signal with no waiter is lost.

L18 · Concurrency bugs, deadlock & event-based concurrency

Question Answer What are the two main kinds of non-deadlock concurrency bugs? Atomicity violations (a sequence assumed atomic isn't) and order violations (an assumed ordering isn't enforced). List the four conditions for deadlock. Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. What is the most practical way to prevent deadlock? Break circular wait by acquiring locks in a fixed global order (e.g. by address). What's livelock and how do you reduce it? Threads keep failing trylock, releasing and retrying without progress. Add a random delay before retrying. Prevention vs avoidance vs detection? Prevention: design so a deadlock condition can't hold. Avoidance: schedule so deadlock can't happen given known lock needs. Detection: let it happen, find cycles, recover. Why must event handlers never block? There's one thread; a blocking call stops the whole server from handling any other event. What's a continuation in event-based programming? Saved state needed to finish handling an event later, e.g. after async I/O completes.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
L19 · I/O devices

Question Answer What are the three registers of the canonical device interface? Status, command, data. When is polling better than interrupts? When the device is fast, so the first poll usually finds it done; interrupt handling and context switching would cost more. What is interrupt livelock? A flood of interrupts (e.g. network packets) keeps the CPU busy handling interrupts so no real work gets done. What does DMA do? A DMA engine transfers data between memory and a device without the CPU copying it, then raises an interrupt when finished. Two ways the OS can access device registers? Privileged I/O instructions (in/out) or memory-mapped I/O. Why are device drivers a reliability problem? They make up most of the kernel's code (~70% of Linux), are often written by less experienced developers, and run in kernel mode.

L20 · Hard disks (and SSDs in brief)

Question Answer What's the disk I/O time formula? T_I/O = T_seek + T_rotation + T_transfer. Average rotational delay at 15,000 RPM? One rotation = 4 ms, so average = 2 ms (half a rotation). Roughly how much faster is sequential than random I/O on a hard disk? About 200–300×, e.g. 125 MB/s vs 0.66 MB/s. What's the problem with SSTF? Starvation of requests on far tracks; it also ignores rotational delay. What does SPTF do differently, and where is it implemented? Picks the request with the least seek + rotation time; implemented inside the drive, which knows the head position and geometry. What write is guaranteed atomic on a disk? A single 512-byte sector write. Why do SSDs need a flash translation layer? Flash must erase whole blocks before reprogramming pages and blocks wear out, so the FTL remaps writes log-style to fresh pages, garbage-collects and wear-levels.

L21 · RAID

Question Answer What does RAID-0 provide and not provide? Striping for full capacity and performance; no redundancy (any failure loses data). How does parity let RAID-4/5 recover a failed disk? Parity is the XOR of the stripe's data blocks; XOR-ing the surviving blocks and parity reconstructs the missing one. How many I/Os does a small write need in RAID-4/5, and why? Four: read old data and old parity, write new data and new parity (subtractive parity). Why is RAID-4 slow for small random writes? Every write must update the single parity disk, which serializes all writes (total R/2). How does RAID-5 fix RAID-4's problem? It rotates parity across all disks, so small writes to different stripes can proceed in parallel (N/4·R). Why is RAID-1's sequential read only N/2·S? Each disk serves every other block; it rotates past blocks its mirror is serving, so it delivers only half its bandwidth. Capacity of RAID-1, RAID-4, RAID-5 with N disks of B blocks? RAID-1: N·B/2. RAID-4 and RAID-5: (N−1)·B.

L22 · Files & directories (the API)

Question Answer What is an inode number? The file's low-level name; the file system uses it to find the inode (metadata and block pointers). What does a directory contain? A list of (name, inode number) pairs, including "." and "..". When do two file descriptors share an offset? When they refer to the same open-file-table entry: after fork() or dup(). Separate open() calls get separate offsets. Why call fsync()? write() buffers data in memory; fsync forces it (and metadata) to persistent storage. How do you update a file atomically? Write a temporary file, fsync it, then rename() it over the original; rename is atomic. Hard link vs symbolic link? Hard link: another name for the same inode (refcount). Symlink: a file containing a path; can cross file systems and point to directories, but can dangle. Why is the call to remove a file named unlink()? It removes one name (link) to the inode; the file is freed only when the link count drops to zero.

L23 · File system implementation (VSFS)

Question Answer Name the five regions of VSFS's on-disk layout. Superblock, inode bitmap, data bitmap, inode table, data region. What's in an inode? Metadata (type, size, owner, permissions, times, link count, block count) and pointers to data blocks. Max file size with 12 direct pointers, one indirect block, 4 KB blocks, 4-byte pointers? (12 + 1024) × 4 KB = 4144 KB ≈ 4 MB. Why does a multi-level (imbalanced) tree make sense for inodes? Most files are small and fit in direct pointers; the rare large files use indirect blocks. How many reads to open /foo/bar (no cache)? Five: root inode, root data, foo inode, foo data, bar inode. Why does reading a file cause a write? The inode's last-access time must be updated. Three benefits of write buffering? Batching updates into fewer I/Os, better scheduling of writes, and avoiding writes entirely for short-lived files. Extents vs pointers? An extent is a start pointer plus a length, describing a contiguous run with little metadata; pointers name each block but are more flexible.

L24 · FFS: locality and the Fast File System

Question Answer Why was the original UNIX file system so slow? It ignored disk geometry: inodes far from data (long seeks), a fragmented free list, and tiny 512-byte blocks. What is a cylinder (block) group? A contiguous region of the disk with its own copy of the superblock, inode and data bitmaps, inodes and data blocks. Where does FFS place a new file and a new directory? File: same group as its parent directory, with its data near its inode. Directory: a group with few directories and many free inodes. Why does FFS spread large files across groups? So one big file doesn't fill a group and destroy locality for other related files; chunks are large enough to amortise the seeks. What are sub-blocks for? 512-byte allocations for small files to avoid internal fragmentation with 4 KB blocks.

L25 · Crash consistency: fsck & journaling

Question Answer Which three blocks must be written to append one data block? The inode, the data bitmap, and the data block. What's the main drawback of fsck? It scans the entire disk, so recovery takes time proportional to disk size — far too slow for large disks. List the steps of data journaling. Journal write (TxB + contents), journal commit (TxE), checkpoint (write in place), free the journal space. Why must TxE be written separately, after the rest? The disk can reorder writes; if TxE lands first and the crash hits, recovery could replay garbage. TxE fits in one sector, so its write is atomic. What does recovery do with the journal? Replays (redoes) every committed transaction — those with a TxE — and ignores incomplete ones. In ordered metadata journaling, when is user data written? To its final location before the journal commit, so metadata never points to garbage. What rule underlies crash-consistent write ordering? Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it. Why do metadata journaling instead of data journaling? Data journaling writes all data twice, halving write bandwidth; metadata is small.

L26 · Log-structured file systems & data integrity

Question Answer What's the core idea of LFS? Buffer all updates (data and metadata) in memory and write them sequentially as large segments to free space; never overwrite in place. Why does LFS need an inode map? Inodes move every time they're written, so the imap records each inode's current location. How does LFS find the imap? Through the checkpoint region, a fixed location that points to the latest imap pieces; it's updated periodically. How does the LFS cleaner decide if a block is live? The segment summary block gives the block's inode number and offset; if that inode (via the imap) still points to this address, it's live. What is a latent sector error vs silent corruption? LSE: the disk detects the bad sector and returns an error. Silent corruption: the disk returns wrong data with no error. How do you detect misdirected writes? Store the disk and sector address alongside the checksum and verify it on read. What is disk scrubbing? Periodically reading all blocks and verifying checksums to find corruption early.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
L27 · Distributed systems, NFS & AFS

Question Answer How do you build reliable communication over an unreliable network? Acknowledgements, timeouts with retries, and sequence numbers to detect duplicates (plus checksums for corruption). What does an RPC stub do? Marshals arguments into a message, sends it, waits for the reply and unmarshals the result, so a remote call looks like a local one. Why is NFSv2 stateless, and what does that buy? Every request carries all needed information, so after a server crash clients simply retry — no state to rebuild. What's in an NFS file handle? Volume ID, inode number, generation number. What does idempotent mean, and why does NFS need it? Performing an operation more than once has the same effect as once; it makes retrying after timeouts safe. What are the two cache-consistency problems? Update visibility (when do others see my writes) and stale cache (is my cached copy out of date). What is an AFS callback? A promise from the server to notify a client when a file it caches is modified, so the client needn't ask the server on each open. Why must an NFS server commit writes to disk before replying? If it replied first and crashed, the client would think the data was safe when it was lost.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
All 296 terms used in the lessons. On the website, every one of these terms has a dotted underline: hover over it (or tap it on a phone) to see this definition without leaving the page.

To add or change a definition, edit includes/glossary.md and re-run python scripts/build_flashcards.py.

Term Meaning address space A process's private view of memory: code, heap and stack at virtual addresses AFS Andrew File System — whole-file caching with server callbacks allotment In MLFQ, how much CPU time a job may use at one priority level before it is demoted AMAT Average memory access time = T_M + P_miss × T_D argc Argument count — how many words were typed to start the program (including the program name) argv Argument vector — array of the command-line words as strings; argv[0] is the program name ASID Address-space identifier — tags TLB entries with their process so the TLB needn't be flushed on a switch async I/O I/O that returns immediately; completion is checked later or signalled atomic All or nothing — can't be interrupted partway atomicity The property of executing all at once, as one indivisible step atomicity violation A sequence that should be atomic isn't protected attribute cache NFS client cache of file attributes, valid for a few seconds B-tree A balanced, wide tree used for fast lookups on disk (databases, file systems) Banker's algorithm Dijkstra's deadlock-avoidance algorithm: only grant requests that keep the system in a safe state base and bounds Translation with two registers: physical = virtual + base; fault if virtual ≥ bounds Belady's anomaly With FIFO, adding cache space can increase misses best fit Allocate from the smallest free chunk that is big enough binary semaphore A semaphore initialised to 1, used as a lock bitmap One bit per inode or block: free or in use block The file system's unit of storage, typically 4 KB block group ext2/3/4's name for a cylinder group bounded buffer Fixed-size shared buffer between producers and consumers buddy allocator Splits memory in powers of two; a freed block merges with its 'buddy' if that is free bus The shared wires that connect the CPU, memory and devices C-SCAN Circular SCAN — sweep in one direction only, then jump back to the start cache Small, fast memory holding copies of recently used data so it needn't be fetched again from somewhere slower cache affinity A process runs faster on the CPU it last ran on, because that CPU's cache is still warm cache coherence Hardware that keeps multiple CPU caches consistent with each other callback A server's promise to tell a client when a file it caches changes CAS Compare-and-swap — atomic: if *ptr equals expected, store new; return the old value CFS Completely Fair Scheduler (Linux) — runs the process with the lowest virtual runtime checkpoint Writing journaled updates to their final on-disk locations checkpoint region LFS's fixed location that points to the latest pieces of the inode map checkpointing Writing journaled updates to their final on-disk locations checksum Small value computed from data to detect corruption chunk size How many blocks go on one disk before moving to the next disk in a stripe circular wait A cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource the next one holds — a deadlock condition CISC Complex instruction set computer — CPUs with many complex instructions (x86) cleaner LFS garbage collector: compacts live blocks from old segments Clock LRU approximation: a hand sweeps pages, clearing use bits, and evicts the first with use bit 0 coalescing Merging adjacent free chunks into one bigger chunk command-line arguments The words typed after a program's name when starting it, docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Short pages to read before the first lesson:

  • Background you need — 10 minutes on CPU, memory, stack, heap, registers, argc/argv and system calls. Skip it if those are already familiar.
  • The 80/20 map — all 50 chapters sorted into Must, Skim and Skip.
  • The recall system — the 5-step loop, story chains, and the spaced review schedule.
  • 3-week plan — one lesson a day, with reviews already scheduled.

What you need: the free book from ostep.org, a notebook for blurting, and optionally Anki and Python 3 for the homework simulators.

What you don't need: to read every page. Trust the map.

docs.title: The 80/20 map
docs.text:
Every chapter of OSTEP, sorted into three tiers.

  • 🔴 Must — read the chapter's marked sections, do the recall, do the homework simulator if there is one. These carry ~80% of exam and interview questions.
  • 🟡 Skim — read the lesson here, look at the figures in the book, skip the prose.
  • ⚪ Skip — dialogues, history, deep case studies. Come back only if you're curious.

docs.title: Why this split works
docs.text:
Three ideas show up again and again across the whole book. If you understand them, the 🟡 chapters mostly become "the same idea, applied again":

  1. Mechanism vs. policy. How something is done (context switch, page table walk) is separate from which choice is made (which process runs, which page is evicted). Every Part I chapter is one or the other.
  2. Add a level of indirection, then cache it. Virtual → physical addresses, then the TLB. File name → inode → blocks, then the buffer cache. Inode map in LFS.
  3. Make the common case fast, and handle the rare case correctly. Direct execution with traps, TLB hits vs. misses, journaling that only writes metadata twice.

docs.title: Background you need (10 minutes)
docs.text:
OSTEP assumes you know a little about how a computer runs a program. If words like register, stack or pointer feel fuzzy, read this page first. Everything else in the course builds on these ideas.

Hover over underlined words

On this website, any word with a dotted underline has a definition. Hover over it with the mouse, or tap it on a phone. The full list is in the Glossary.

docs.title: 1 · The three parts of a computer
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CPU["<b>CPU</b><br/>runs instructions<br/>(has registers + cache)"] <--> RAM["<b>Memory (RAM)</b><br/>fast, temporary<br/>lost at power-off"]
    RAM <--> DISK[("<b>Disk / SSD</b><br/>slow, permanent")]
Part Think of it as Speed (rough) CPU The worker who follows a recipe one step at a time One simple step takes under 1 nanosecond Memory (RAM) The kitchen counter: everything currently in use sits here ~100 nanoseconds to fetch something Disk / SSD The storeroom: big and permanent, but far away Hard disk: ~10 milliseconds, 100,000× slower than RAM

That huge speed gap explains a lot of the book. Disks are so slow that the OS works hard to avoid touching them, mostly by keeping copies of data in memory.

Units: 1 KB ≈ a thousand bytes, 1 MB ≈ a million, 1 GB ≈ a billion. In OS work these are powers of two: 1 KB = 1024 bytes and 4 KB = 4096 bytes. A millisecond (ms) is 1/1000 of a second. A microsecond (µs) is 1/1000 of a millisecond. A nanosecond (ns) is 1/1000 of a microsecond.

docs.title: 2 · How the CPU runs a program
docs.text:
A program is a list of instructions: tiny steps like "load a number from memory", "add two numbers" and "store the result in memory".

Inside the CPU are a handful of registers. Each is a tiny, very fast slot that holds one value. Three of them matter most in this course:

  • Program counter (PC) — the address of the next instruction. The CPU fetches that instruction, does it, moves the PC on, and repeats forever.
  • Stack pointer — where the top of the stack is right now (see below).
  • General registers — scratch space for the values being worked on.

Why it matters: if you save all the registers, you've saved "where the program is" in its work. Restore them later and the program carries on as if nothing happened. That's how the OS switches between programs (L03).

docs.title: 3 · Memory: addresses, code, stack and heap
docs.text:
Memory is one long row of numbered bytes. The number is the byte's address.

A running program's memory is split into regions:

Region What lives there Example (C) Code The program's instructions — Static data Global variables int count = 0; outside any function Stack Local variables, function arguments and return addresses. Grows when a function is called and shrinks when it returns int x = 5; inside a function Heap Memory the program asks for while running and gives back when done p = malloc(100); … free(p); (Java: new)

A pointer is just a variable that holds an address. int *p means "p holds the address of an int".

docs.title: 4 · Just enough C to read the code in this course
docs.text:
The book's examples are in C. You don't need to write C; you only need to read short snippets.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {     // program starts here
    printf("I was started as %s\n", argv[0]);
    for (int i = 1; i < argc; i++)
        printf("argument %d: %s\n", i, argv[i]);
    return 0;                          // 0 = "finished OK"
}
  • main is where every C program starts.
  • argc (argument count) is how many words you typed to start the program.
  • argv (argument vector) holds those words as text. argv[0] is the program's own name.
  • Running ./show hello world prints I was started as ./show, then argument 1: hello and argument 2: world. Here argc = 3.
  • Java's public static void main(String[] args) is the same idea, except args doesn't include the program name.

Other things you'll see:

C Meaning x++ add 1 to x int *p p is a pointer to an int *p = 5 store 5 at the address in p &x the address of x p->field the field of the struct p points to while (cond) ; loop doing nothing until cond is false ("spinning") NULL "points nowhere"

docs.title: 5 · The OS, the kernel and system calls
docs.text:
• The kernel is the core of the operating system. It runs in a special, all-powerful CPU mode called kernel mode.
  • Your programs run in user mode, which isn't allowed to touch hardware directly.
  • When a program needs something only the OS may do (read a file, start a process), it makes a system call. That is a special instruction that jumps safely into the kernel, which does the job and then returns.

Think of a bank: you (user mode) can't walk into the vault. You fill in a form at the counter (system call), and the teller (kernel) does it for you.

docs.title: 6 · Files you already know: stdin, stdout, stderr
docs.text:
Every program starts with three open "files":

  • stdin (number 0) — input, usually the keyboard.
  • stdout (number 1) — normal output, usually the screen.
  • stderr (number 2) — error messages.

In a shell, ls > out.txt sends stdout to a file. ls | wc -l connects the stdout of ls to the stdin of wc.

docs.title: 7 · Caches, in one paragraph
docs.text: A cache is a small, fast place that keeps copies of things you used recently, so the next use is quick. Your browser caches web pages; the CPU caches memory; the OS caches disk blocks in RAM. Caches work because programs tend to reuse the same data soon (temporal locality) and to use data next to what they just used (spatial locality). You'll meet this idea in almost every lesson.

docs.title: Ready?
docs.text: If the ideas above make sense, start with L01 · Intro & the three pieces. Come back here whenever a lesson assumes something you're unsure of.

docs.title: The recall system
docs.text: Reading feels like learning, but most of it is gone within a week. What makes things stick is pulling them out of your head (retrieval) at growing intervals (spacing). This page is the whole method. It takes 5 minutes to read and adds about 15 minutes to each lesson.

docs.title: The 5-step loop (per lesson)
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["1 · Preview<br/>TL;DR + big question<br/>2 min"] --> B["2 · Read<br/>lesson + 🔴 book sections<br/>30–40 min"]
    B --> C["3 · Blurt<br/>book closed, write<br/>everything — 5 min"]
    C --> D["4 · Check & fix<br/>compare, mark gaps<br/>5 min"]
    D --> E["5 · Explain<br/>60-second talk<br/>out loud"]
    E -.next day.-> F["Flashcards<br/>+1 · +3 · +7 · +21 days"]

docs.title: 1 · Preview (2 min)
docs.text: Read only the In plain words box, the TL;DR and The big question. You now know the question before you read the answer, so your brain files new details under it.

docs.title: 2 · Read
docs.text: Read the lesson, then the book sections marked 🔴 in "Read in the book". Don't highlight. Instead, after every section, look away and say one sentence about what it did.

docs.title: 3 · Blurt (the most important step)
docs.text: Close everything. On a blank page, write down everything you remember: the story chain, the diagram, the rules, the numbers. Messy is fine. This feels hard — that difficulty is what builds memory.

docs.title: 4 · Check & fix
docs.text: Open the lesson. With a different colour, add what you missed. Those gaps are your flashcards. Star anything you got wrong.

docs.title: 5 · Explain (Feynman test)
docs.text: Each lesson ends with an "Explain it" prompt. Answer it out loud in 60 seconds, as if to a friend who knows programming but not OS. If you say "it just sort of…", that's a gap — go back to that part.

docs.title: The story chain — your main memory hook
docs.text:
OSTEP almost always teaches by trying something simple, showing how it breaks, and fixing it. Each lesson writes this down as a chain:

Problem → naive fix → ❌ what breaks → better fix → ❌ what breaks → … → final design

Chains are far easier to remember than lists of facts, because each step causes the next. If you can rebuild the chain from memory, you can rebuild the details. In an exam, write the chain first, then fill in.

Example (scheduling): Run jobs in order (FIFO) → ❌ a long job blocks short ones (convoy) → run shortest first (SJF) → ❌ a long job already running still blocks late arrivals → preempt (STCF) → ❌ interactive users wait → time slices (Round Robin) → ❌ we don't know job lengths → learn from history (MLFQ).

The big chain map has every chain on one page.

docs.title: Spaced review schedule
docs.text:
After the lesson day (Day 0), review at these gaps. Each review is 5 minutes: flip the flashcards, redo the blurt for the chain only.

Review When What R1 Day +1 Flashcards + blurt the chain R2 Day +3 Flashcards only, starred cards twice R3 Day +7 One "Explain it" out loud + drills for that part R4 Day +21 Mixed drills across all parts

The easiest way to run this is Anki: import the deck from Flashcards and it schedules everything for you.

docs.title: Four more tricks that pay off
docs.text:
Interleave. After the first week, don't review one topic at a time. Mix questions from scheduling, paging and locks in one sitting. It feels worse and works better, because exams mix too. The mixed drills are built for this.

Run the simulators. OSTEP's homework comes with small Python simulators (ostep-homework). Each one generates a problem with a random seed (-s 1, -s 2, …) and shows the answer with -c. Solve a few seeds in your head first, then check. This is retrieval practice with infinite questions. Every lesson lists the right simulator.

File it under mechanism or policy. When you meet a new idea, ask: is this how (mechanism) or which (policy)? Two mental drawers make recall faster.

Draw, don't copy. Redraw each lesson's diagram from memory once. If you can draw the page table walk or the journaling timeline, you understand it.

docs.title: Signs it's working

docs.title: L01 · Intro & the three pieces
docs.text:
Book: Ch 2 (pp. 3–19) · Priority: 🟡 good to know · Time: 20 min

In plain words

Picture a busy hotel. Guests (programs) each feel they have a private room, their own staff and their own safe. In reality there is one building and one staff, shared cleverly. The hotel manager (the OS) does three jobs:

  • Virtualization: makes shared things look private. One CPU feels like many; one memory feels like your own.
  • Concurrency: many guests act at once without trampling each other.
  • Persistence: valuables locked in the safe survive a power cut.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• An OS is a layer of software that virtualizes hardware (CPU, memory, disk) so every program thinks it has the machine to itself.
  • It also manages concurrency (many things happening at once) and persistence (data that survives power loss).
  • Programs ask the OS for things through system calls; the OS is effectively a resource manager and a standard library.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How does the OS turn physical resources into general, powerful, easy-to-use virtual ones — efficiently and safely?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Programs want the whole machine → give each one the real hardware → ❌ only one can run, any bug crashes everything → a layer that hands out slices of the hardware and enforces rules → the operating system: virtualization for sharing, protection for isolation, persistence for safety.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
Virtualizing the CPU. Run four programs on one CPU and all four seem to make progress. The OS switches between them fast enough that each looks like it owns a processor. (Mechanism: L03. Policy: L04.)

Virtualizing memory. Two copies of the same program can both print "my variable is at address 0x200000" (an address written in hexadecimal) and yet change different values, because each sees its own private copy. Each process has its own private virtual address space; the OS and hardware map it onto real memory. (L06 onward.)

Concurrency. Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter a million times. Expected result 2,000,000; actual result is often less, and different every run. Why: counter++ looks like one step but the CPU does it in three — load the value from memory, add 1, store it back. If the OS switches threads in the middle, both threads may load the same old value, and one update is lost. (L13.)

Persistence. Memory is lost at power off, so data goes to disk through the file system. Writing safely is hard: for speed the OS holds writes in memory for a while and sends them to disk in batches, and it must not leave the disk broken if the power dies halfway through. (L22 onward.)

docs.title: The design goals (remember the five)
docs.text:
Goal Meaning Abstraction Easy-to-use interfaces (process, address space, file) Performance The OS itself should use little CPU time and memory (low overhead) Protection / isolation One program can't harm another or the OS Reliability The OS itself must not crash Energy, security, mobility Increasingly important extras 
flowchart TB
    subgraph User["User mode"]
        A[Program A] & B[Program B] & C[Program C]
    end
    subgraph Kernel["Kernel mode — the OS"]
        S[Scheduler] --- M[Memory manager] --- F[File system]
    end
    A & B & C -- system calls / traps --> Kernel
    Kernel --> HW[(CPU · RAM · Disk)]

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• "OS = the kernel and the desktop apps" — no. In this book, OS means the kernel: the core part that shares out the hardware and protects programs from each other.
  • A system call is not a normal function call: it switches the CPU into kernel mode via a trap, so the OS can do privileged things.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory (5 min): name the three pieces with one example each, and the five design goals.

What are the "three easy pieces"?

Virtualization, concurrency, persistence.

Why can two processes print the same address for a variable yet hold different values?

Each has its own virtual address space; the same virtual address maps to different physical memory.

Why does a shared counter incremented by two threads end up wrong?

counter++ is load–add–store. If a context switch hits between them, one thread's update overwrites the other's. The three instructions are not atomic.

How does a system call differ from a procedure call?

It traps into the kernel and raises the hardware privilege level, so the OS can perform restricted operations; a procedure call stays in user mode.

Explain it out loud (60 seconds, as if to a friend): "Why do we need an operating system at all? What would break without one?"

docs.title: L02 · Processes & fork / exec / wait
docs.text:
Book: Ch 4–5 (pp. 25–48) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 45 min · Simulators: cpu-intro/process-run.py, cpu-api/fork.py

In plain words

A program is a recipe sitting in a book (a file on disk). A process is someone actually cooking that recipe right now. They have ingredients on the counter (memory), are at a particular step (the program counter) and have tools in hand (open files).

You can have several cooks following the same recipe at once: two terminal windows running the same program are two processes.

  • fork() = clone the cook, half-made dish and all.
  • exec() = the clone throws away the recipe and starts a different one.
  • wait() = the original cook waits until the clone is finished.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• A process is a running program: its memory (address space), its registers (incl. PC and stack pointer) and its open files.
  • A process moves between three main states: Running ⇄ Ready, and Running → Blocked → Ready when it waits for I/O.
  • UNIX creates processes with fork() (copy me), exec() (replace me with another program) and wait() (let my child finish). Splitting fork from exec is what makes shells powerful.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How do we create and control processes, and how does the OS give the illusion of many CPUs?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Want many programs at once → one CPU, one program → ❌ CPU idles while waiting for disk → time-share: switch between processes → need to save/restore each process's state → keep it in a process control block (PCB) in a process list → need an API to create them → fork + exec + wait.

docs.title: What makes up a process (machine state)
docs.text:
• Memory (the address space):
    • code — the program's instructions;
    • static data — global variables, e.g. int count = 0; outside any function;
    • heap — memory the program asks for while running (malloc in C, new in Java);
    • stack — local variables, function arguments and return addresses; it grows on each call and shrinks on return.
  • Registers (tiny, super-fast storage inside the CPU):
    • program counter (PC) — address of the next instruction to run;
    • stack pointer — where the top of the stack is right now;
    • frame pointer — where the current function's stack area starts;
    • general registers — scratch values the code is working on.
  • I/O state: the list of open files. Every process starts with three: 0 = stdin (keyboard input), 1 = stdout (normal output), 2 = stderr (error output).

Never seen a C main before? 30-second detour

A C program starts at int main(int argc, char *argv[]). These two parameters carry the command-line arguments — the words you typed to start the program.

  • argc = argument count: how many words.
  • argv = argument vector: an array of those words as strings. argv[0] is the program's own name.

Typing ./copy a.txt b.txt gives argc = 3 and argv = ["./copy", "a.txt", "b.txt"]. (Java's main(String[] args) is the same idea: args.length ≈ argc, args ≈ argv.)

The OS is the one that puts these words into the new process's memory — that's why they show up in step 2 below.

docs.title: How a program becomes a process
docs.text:
1. Load the code and static data from the executable file on disk into memory. Modern OSes do this lazily: they load a piece (a page) only when the program first touches it, so programs start fast.
  2. Create the stack and place argc and argv on it, so main finds its arguments; create a small heap for later malloc calls.
  3. Open the three standard files (stdin, stdout, stderr — fds 0, 1, 2).
  4. Jump to main(): set the PC to the program's first instruction, switch to user mode, and let it run.

    D[("Disk:<br/>program file")] -- "1 · load code + data<br/>(lazily)" --> M
    subgraph M["Memory: new address space"]
        direction TB
        C[code + static data]
        H["heap (small, for malloc)"]
        S["stack: argc, argv"]
    end
    M -- "3 · fds 0/1/2 opened<br/>4 · PC = main, run" --> CPU[(CPU)]

docs.title: Process states
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Ready: created
    Ready --> Running: scheduled
    Running --> Ready: descheduled (timer)
    Running --> Blocked: I/O started
    Blocked --> Ready: I/O done
    Running --> Zombie: exit()
    Zombie --> [*]: parent calls wait()

What the states mean:

  • Running — on the CPU right now.
  • Ready — could run, but waiting for its turn on the CPU.
  • Blocked — waiting for something slow (disk, keyboard, network); can't run even if the CPU is free.
  • Zombie — finished, but its parent hasn't yet asked "how did it go?" (collected its exit status with wait()).

docs.title: The process API
Why fork and exec are separate
docs.text:
The gap between fork() and exec() lets the shell change the child's environment before the new program starts. That's how redirection works:

When you type wc notes.txt > out.txt:

  1. The shell forks a child.
  2. The child closes file descriptor 1 (stdout, normally the screen).
  3. The child opens out.txt. The OS always hands out the lowest free number, which is now 1, so out.txt becomes stdout.
  4. The child execs wc. wc writes to stdout as usual, without knowing it's now writing into a file.

Pipes (ls | wc) use the same trick: the shell connects one child's stdout to the other's stdin before calling exec.

docs.title: Other bits
docs.text:
• kill() sends a signal — a short message to a process. Pressing Ctrl-C sends SIGINT ("please stop"); Ctrl-Z sends SIGTSTP ("pause"). A program can choose to catch a signal and react, using signal().
  • You can only signal your own processes. The superuser (root), the administrator account, can signal anyone.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
printf("hello\n");
int rc = fork();
printf("rc=%d\n", rc);

Output: hello once (it was printed before the fork, when there was only one process), then two rc= lines — rc=0 from the child and rc=<some number> from the parent (the child's process ID). The order of the two lines is not fixed: the scheduler decides who runs first. Add wait() in the parent and the child's line always comes first.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• After fork(), the child gets a copy of memory. Changing a variable in the child does not change the parent's.
  • exec() does not create a new process. The PID stays the same.
  • Output order after fork() is nondeterministic without wait().
  • Lazy loading means "load the program" doesn't read the whole file up front.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: draw the state diagram; write the fork–exec–wait snippet; explain > redirection in 3 steps.

What does fork() return in the parent and in the child?

Child's PID in the parent; 0 in the child; −1 on failure.

When does exec() return?

Only if it fails. On success the calling program is replaced and the old code is gone.

Why does UNIX split process creation into fork() and exec()?

So code can run in the child between the two, to set up redirection, pipes or other environment changes before the new program starts.

What are the three main process states and their transitions?

Running, Ready, Blocked. Running→Ready (descheduled), Ready→Running (scheduled), Running→Blocked (I/O starts), Blocked→Ready (I/O done).

What is a zombie process?

One that has exited but whose parent hasn't called wait() to collect its exit status.

What does the OS store in a process control block (PCB)?

Saved registers (context), state, PID, parent, memory info, open files, and similar per-process data.

docs.title: L03 · Limited direct execution
docs.text:
Book: Ch 6 (pp. 49–62) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 40 min

In plain words

Think of a driving instructor with a learner. For speed, the learner drives the real car directly (programs run on the real CPU). But the instructor keeps dual controls:

  • Some actions need permission. The learner can't take the motorway alone, so they ask (a system call).
  • An alarm rings every few minutes (the timer interrupt), and the instructor can take over the wheel. That stops a learner from driving off forever.
  • Swapping learners means writing down exactly where the first one was (seat, mirrors, route) so they can carry on later. That's a context switch.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• For speed, the OS lets programs run directly on the CPU. For control, it limits them: user programs run in user mode and must trap into the kernel for privileged work.
  • The kernel regains the CPU through a timer interrupt, even if a program never gives it up.
  • Switching processes = context switch: save the old process's registers into its kernel structure, restore the next one's, return from trap.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text:
How can the OS run programs efficiently while keeping control of the CPU?

Two sub-problems: (1) restricted operations — how does a process do I/O without being able to do anything? (2) switching — how does the OS get the CPU back to run someone else?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Run the program directly → ❌ it could do anything (wipe disk) → user mode vs kernel mode; privileged work via system calls that trap → ❌ how does the OS ever run again if a program loops forever? → cooperative: wait for the program to make a syscall or yield → ❌ an infinite loop never yields; only fix is reboot → non-cooperative: a hardware timer interrupt every few ms hands control to the OS → limited direct execution + context switch.

docs.title: Problem 1 — restricted operations
docs.text:
The problem: if a program runs directly on the CPU, what stops it from doing anything it likes, such as erasing the disk or reading another program's memory?

  • The hardware has two modes. In user mode (where programs run), dangerous instructions like talking to the disk are simply refused. In kernel mode (where the OS runs), everything is allowed.
  • So how does a program read a file? It makes a system call. That executes a special trap instruction, which does three things at once: saves the program's registers, switches the CPU to kernel mode, and jumps into the OS.
  • Jumps where? Not anywhere the program chooses. That would let it skip the OS's safety checks. At boot, the OS gives the hardware a trap table: a list of "for event X, run OS code at address Y". A program only says which service it wants by number (e.g. "system call #2 = open a file").
  • Going back: when the OS is done, it runs return-from-trap. This restores the registers, switches back to user mode and resumes the program right after its system call.

docs.title: Problem 2 — switching between processes
docs.text:
The problem: while a program runs, the OS isn't running at all. The CPU only does one thing at a time. So how does the OS ever get the CPU back to let another program have a turn?

  • Cooperative approach (old Mac OS): wait politely. The OS only runs when the program makes a system call, voluntarily gives up the CPU (yields), or crashes. But a program stuck in an infinite loop never does any of those, and the only fix is rebooting the machine.
  • Non-cooperative approach (every modern OS): a hardware timer interrupts the CPU every few milliseconds, whatever the program is doing. The interrupt forces a jump into the OS. Now the OS can decide: let this program continue, or switch to another one.
  • Deciding who runs next is the scheduler's job (L04). The act of switching is a context switch: save the current program's registers, load the next program's registers.

docs.title: The timeline of a context switch (A → B)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Process A (user)
    participant HW as Hardware
    participant OS as OS (kernel)
    participant B as Process B (user)
    A->>A: running...
    HW->>HW: timer interrupt
    HW->>OS: save A's user regs (kernel stack),<br/>kernel mode, jump to handler
    OS->>OS: scheduler picks B
    OS->>OS: switch(): save A's kernel regs → A's PCB,<br/>load B's from B's PCB, use B's kernel stack
    OS->>HW: return-from-trap
    HW->>B: restore B's user regs,<br/>user mode, jump to B's PC
    B->>B: running...

How to read this: time flows downward. A is running; the timer fires; the OS decides to run B instead; it swaps the saved registers; B continues exactly where it last stopped.

Two saves happen:

  1. The hardware saves A's user registers automatically when the interrupt hits.
  2. The OS saves the registers it was using in its own code, in a routine usually called switch(), into A's process control block.

Restoring B is the same two steps in reverse.

docs.title: Costs to remember
docs.text: A system call or context switch takes about a microsecond or less on modern machines, which is cheap. The bigger hidden cost: after a switch, the CPU's caches and TLB are full of the old program's data, so the new program runs slowly for a while until they warm up.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• The trap table is set up at boot, in kernel mode — not by each program.
  • User programs pass a syscall number, not a handler address.
  • "Who saves the registers?" → both: hardware (user registers, on trap/interrupt) and OS (kernel registers, on switch).
  • What if an interrupt happens while handling an interrupt? The OS may disable interrupts briefly and uses locks on its own data — a preview of concurrency.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: write the two problems and their solutions; draw the context-switch timeline with who-saves-what.

What does "limited direct execution" mean?

Run the program directly on the CPU for speed, but limit it: user mode, traps for privileged operations, and a timer interrupt so the OS regains control.

What is the trap table and when is it set up?

A table of handler addresses for traps/interrupts. The kernel installs it at boot using a privileged instruction.

Why does the cooperative approach fail?

A process stuck in an infinite loop never makes a syscall, so the OS never runs again; you must reboot.

How does the OS regain control in the non-cooperative approach?

A hardware timer interrupt every few milliseconds jumps into the OS's interrupt handler.

In a context switch, which registers does the hardware save and which does the OS save?

Hardware saves the user registers onto the process's kernel stack on the interrupt. The OS saves the kernel registers into the process's PCB in switch().

Why pass a system-call number instead of an address?

So user code can only reach approved kernel entry points; it can't jump into the middle of the kernel.

Explain it out loud (60 seconds, as if to a friend): "Your program runs while(1);. Explain step by step how the OS still gets to run another program."

docs.title: L04 · Scheduling basics: FIFO, SJF, STCF, RR
docs.text:
Book: Ch 7 (pp. 63–74) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 45 min · Simulator: cpu-sched/scheduler.py

In plain words

You're at a supermarket with one checkout (one CPU). Who goes first?

  • FIFO: strict arrival order. One person with a full trolley makes everyone with one item wait.
  • SJF / STCF: let people with fewer items go first. Great on average, but the full-trolley person may wait a long time.
  • Round Robin: scan 1 item per customer in turn. Everyone gets started quickly, but everyone finishes late.

There's no single best rule. It depends on whether you care about finishing fast (turnaround) or starting fast (response).

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Two metrics fight each other: turnaround time (finish − arrival) favours running short jobs to completion; response time (first run − arrival) favours switching often.
  • SJF/STCF are optimal for average turnaround; Round Robin is great for response time but nearly the worst for turnaround.
  • Overlap I/O by treating each CPU burst as its own job. And in reality we don't know job lengths — that's what MLFQ (L05) fixes.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How should we design a scheduling policy? What assumptions and metrics matter?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Start with unrealistic assumptions — all jobs arrive together, run the same time, no I/O, length known — and relax them one by one:

FIFO → ❌ (jobs differ in length) a long job in front makes everyone wait — the convoy effect → SJF (run shortest first) → ❌ (jobs arrive at different times) a short job arriving just after a long one starts still waits → STCF (preempt; run the job with the least time remaining) → ❌ (users are interactive) response time is terrible → Round Robin (time slices) → ❌ turnaround now awful; (jobs do I/O) → overlap: run another job while one waits → ❌ (we don't know lengths) → MLFQ.

docs.title: How do we score a scheduler? (metrics)
docs.text:
In this chapter a job just means a process that needs some CPU time.

Metric Formula In words Who cares Turnaround time Tcompletion − Tarrival How long from "job arrives" to "job is finished" Batch work (e.g. a long calculation) Response time Tfirst run − Tarrival How long from "job arrives" to "job first gets the CPU" People typing or clicking Fairness e.g. Jain's index Does everyone get a fair share? Everyone

Lower is better for both times. We usually compare the average across all jobs.

docs.title: The policies
docs.text:
Preemptive means the scheduler can pause a running job to run another one. Non-preemptive means a job runs until it finishes (or blocks).

Policy Preemptive? Good at Bad at FIFO (first in, first out) No Simple Convoy effect: short jobs stuck behind a long one SJF (shortest job first) No Best average turnaround if all jobs arrive together A short job arriving just after a long one starts still waits STCF (shortest time-to-completion first, also called PSJF) Yes Best average turnaround in general Response time; needs to know job lengths RR (round robin) Yes, every time slice Response time, fairness Turnaround (every job finishes late)

docs.title: Round Robin's time slice
docs.text:
A time slice (or quantum) is how long each job runs before RR moves to the next one.

  • It must be a multiple of the timer interrupt period. With a 10 ms timer, slices can be 10, 20, 30 ms…
  • Shorter slice = jobs get started sooner (better response), but more of the CPU's time goes on switching rather than real work.
  • The trade-off in numbers: if one switch costs 1 ms, a 10 ms slice wastes about 10% of the CPU on switching; a 100 ms slice wastes about 1%. Spreading a fixed cost over more work is called amortizing it.
  • Switching also throws away "warm" state: caches and the TLB were full of the old job's data.

docs.title: Incorporating I/O
docs.text:
Real jobs alternate between using the CPU and waiting for I/O (disk, network). When job A starts a disk read, it's blocked and can't use the CPU, so run job B meanwhile. Nothing is wasted.

The trick: treat each short stretch of A's CPU use (each CPU burst) as its own little job. Because the bursts are short, STCF runs them first. A gets its next disk request going quickly, and B fills in the gaps. Both the disk and the CPU stay busy.

docs.title: Worked example (do this one by hand)
docs.text:
Three jobs need A = 100 ms, B = 10 ms and C = 10 ms of CPU. All arrive at time 0, in the order A, B, C.

  • FIFO runs A first (0–100), then B (100–110), then C (110–120).
  • SJF runs the short ones first: B (0–10), C (10–20), then A (20–120).
  • Turnaround for each job = its finish time − 0. Response = its start time − 0.
Policy Completion times Avg turnaround Avg response FIFO A 100, B 110, C 120 (100+110+120)/3 = 110 (0+100+110)/3 = 70 SJF B 10, C 20, A 120 (10+20+120)/3 = 50 (0+10+20)/3 = 10

Now make all three jobs 5 ms long and compare RR (1 ms slice) with SJF:

  • RR runs A, B, C, A, B, C, … one millisecond each. A starts at 0, B at 1, C at 2 → average response = (0+1+2)/3 = 1 ms. But they finish at 13, 14, 15 → average turnaround = 14 ms.
  • SJF (same as FIFO here, since all are equal) runs A 0–5, B 5–10, C 10–15. Response = (0+5+10)/3 = 5 ms. Turnaround = (5+10+15)/3 = 10 ms.

RR wins on response, SJF wins on turnaround. That's the whole trade-off in one example.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Turnaround vs response — they're different formulas; exams love mixing them.
  • SJF is optimal only when all jobs arrive together; STCF is the general optimum for turnaround.
  • RR with a tiny slice is not "free" fairness — the switch cost dominates.
  • Response time is measured to the first time the job runs, not to completion.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: write the four assumptions and which policy each relaxation produces; redo the FIFO/SJF example without looking.

Define turnaround time and response time.

Turnaround = completion − arrival. Response = first run − arrival.

What is the convoy effect?

Short jobs stuck waiting behind a long job in FIFO, inflating average turnaround.

What's the difference between SJF and STCF?

SJF is non-preemptive: it picks the shortest job when choosing. STCF preempts the running job whenever a new job has less remaining time.

Why does RR have poor turnaround?

It stretches every job out across many slices, so all jobs finish near the end.

What's the trade-off in choosing RR's time slice?

Shorter = better response but more context-switch overhead; longer amortizes the switch cost but hurts response.

How does the scheduler use I/O to improve utilisation?

When a job blocks on I/O, run another job; treat each CPU burst as a separate job so interactive bursts run quickly and overlap with I/O.

docs.title: L05 · MLFQ, lottery & multiprocessor scheduling
docs.text:
Book: Ch 8 (pp. 75–86) 🔴 · Ch 9 (pp. 87–96) 🟡 · Ch 10 (pp. 97–108) 🟡 · Time: 50 min · Simulators: cpu-sched-mlfq/mlfq.py, cpu-sched-lottery/lottery.py

In plain words

A doctor's waiting room with no appointment times. The receptionist doesn't know who needs 2 minutes and who needs an hour, so she watches and learns:

  • Everyone new starts in the "quick" line.
  • If you keep the doctor busy for a long time, you're moved to a slower line.
  • Every so often, everyone is moved back to the quick line, so nobody waits forever and people whose needs changed get another chance.
  • She counts your total time with the doctor, so you can't cheat by stepping out briefly and coming back.

That is MLFQ. Lottery scheduling is the raffle version: hold 75% of the tickets and you win about 75% of the CPU time.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• MLFQ learns a job's behaviour from history: jobs that use their whole time slice drift down to low priority (CPU-bound), jobs that give up the CPU early stay high (interactive).
  • Two fixes make it safe: priority boost (stop starvation) and better accounting of total time used at a level (stop gaming).
  • Lottery/stride give each job a proportional share using tickets. Multi-CPU scheduling adds cache affinity and load balancing.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can a scheduler minimise turnaround and response time without knowing how long jobs run?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Don't know job lengths → several queues with different priorities; learn from behaviour → new jobs start at the top; drop a job down when it uses a full slice → ❌ starvation: many interactive jobs keep long jobs from ever running; also a job can change from CPU-bound to interactive and be stuck low → Rule 5: periodically boost everyone to the top → ❌ gaming: a job yields just before its slice ends and stays on top forever → Rule 4 rewritten: count total time used at a level, regardless of how many times it yields → final MLFQ.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
MLFQ keeps several queues, each with a priority level. Jobs in a higher queue always run before jobs in a lower one. The clever part is that a job's priority isn't fixed: the scheduler moves jobs between queues based on how they behaved so far.

  • A job that keeps using its full slice is probably a long, CPU-bound job (e.g. a video export), so it moves down.
  • A job that keeps giving up the CPU early, because it's waiting for keyboard or disk, is probably interactive (e.g. a text editor), so it stays high and feels snappy.

docs.title: The five rules (memorise these exactly)
docs.text:
1. If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs.
  2. If Priority(A) = Priority(B), A and B run in round robin.
  3. A new job starts at the highest priority.
  4. Once a job uses up its time allotment at a level (no matter how many times it gave up the CPU), its priority is reduced.
  5. After some period S, move all jobs to the topmost queue.
flowchart TB
    N[New job] --> Q2
    Q2["Q2 — highest · short slice (e.g. 10 ms)"] -- used allotment --> Q1
    Q1["Q1 · medium slice"] -- used allotment --> Q0
    Q0["Q0 — lowest · long slice (e.g. 100+ ms)"]
    Q0 -. every S ms: boost .-> Q2
    Q1 -. every S ms: boost .-> Q2

What each rule is for:

  • Rules 1–2: the basic "higher priority first, take turns at the same level".
  • Rule 3: assume every new job might be short and interactive. If it is, it finishes quickly; if not, it sinks.
  • Rule 4: sinking. Its "no matter how many times" wording stops cheating (see the worked example).
  • Rule 5: the boost. Without it, a steady stream of interactive jobs could keep long jobs from ever running (starvation).

Tuning: high queues get short slices (interactive jobs switch quickly), low queues get long slices (CPU-bound jobs waste less time switching). How often to boost (S) has no perfect value: too rarely and long jobs starve, too often and interactive jobs lose their advantage. Real systems tune it by experiment (Solaris uses a configurable table; FreeBSD computes priority from recent CPU use).

docs.title: Proportional share (Ch 9) — the short version
docs.text:
A different goal: instead of fast turnaround or response, give each job a guaranteed share of the CPU (e.g. "A gets 75%, B gets 25%").

  • Lottery scheduling: each job holds tickets (A has 75, B has 25). Every time slice, draw a random ticket number; whoever holds it runs. Over many draws A wins about 75% of the time. It's simple, but only fair on average: over a short period, B might get lucky or unlucky.
  • Ticket tricks: a user can split their tickets among their own jobs (currency); a job waiting on a server can lend its tickets to that server (transfer); a trusted job can temporarily give itself more (inflation).
  • Stride scheduling: the non-random version. Each job has a stride = (a big number) ÷ (its tickets), so more tickets = smaller stride. Keep a running total (pass) per job. Always run the job with the lowest pass, then add its stride to its pass. Jobs with small strides get picked more often, in exact proportion. Downside: when a new job joins, what pass should it start with? (Lottery has no such problem.)
  • Linux CFS (not in v0.90 of the book — later editions add it; worth knowing for interviews): counts how much CPU each process has had, its virtual runtime, and always runs the process that has had the least. Processes are kept in a sorted tree (a red-black tree) so finding the smallest is fast. Nice values (priorities) make vruntime grow slower for important processes. A target period (sched_latency, e.g. 48 ms) is shared among runnable processes, with a minimum slice (min_granularity, e.g. 6 ms).

docs.title: Multiprocessor scheduling (Ch 10) — the short version
docs.text:
With several CPUs (cores), new issues appear:

  • Each CPU has its own cache. Hardware keeps the caches in agreement with each other (cache coherence), but code that shares data still needs locks.
  • Cache affinity: a process runs faster if it goes back to the same CPU as last time, because that CPU's cache still holds its data.
  • Single-queue (SQMS): one shared list of jobs for all CPUs. Simple and balanced, but every CPU fights over that one list's lock, and jobs hop between CPUs (losing their warm cache).
  • Multi-queue (MQMS): one list per CPU. Scales well and keeps jobs on their CPU, but one CPU can end up busy while another sits idle (load imbalance). Fix: work stealing, where an idle CPU takes jobs from a busy CPU's list.
  • Linux's O(1) and CFS schedulers are multi-queue; BFS was single-queue.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Two jobs: A is CPU-bound (it would happily run for seconds); B is interactive (runs 1 ms, then waits for the keyboard). Three queues, Q2 = top, 10 ms slices.

  • A starts in Q2, uses its full 10 ms → drops to Q1 → uses another full 10 ms → drops to Q0 and stays there.
  • B arrives, starts in Q2, runs 1 ms, then waits for input. When it comes back it's still in Q2, because it hasn't used up its allotment. So B always runs ahead of A: fast response. A runs whenever B is waiting.
  • Cheating ("gaming the scheduler"): suppose A is crafty. It runs 9.9 ms, then does a pointless tiny I/O just before its slice ends, so it never "uses a full slice". Under the book's first draft of Rule 4 (drop only if you use the whole slice), A would stay in Q2 forever and hog the CPU. The final Rule 4 counts total time at a level (9.9 + 9.9 + … ms), so A still drops once it reaches 10 ms.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• The old rules 4a/4b (drop if slice used, stay if you yield) are replaced by the new Rule 4 — know both and why.
  • Boost (Rule 5) solves two problems: starvation and jobs that change behaviour.
  • Lottery is probabilistically fair; short jobs may get unlucky.
  • Stride needs global state; lottery doesn't.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: write all five MLFQ rules, then the two problems each fix (starvation, gaming).

What is MLFQ's key idea?

Use several priority queues and adjust a job's priority based on its observed behaviour, so it approximates SJF without knowing job lengths.

Which MLFQ rule prevents starvation, and what else does it fix?

Rule 5 (periodic priority boost). It also lets a job that became interactive get back to high priority.

How could a program game the original MLFQ, and what fixes it?

Issue an I/O just before its slice ends to stay at high priority. Fixed by accounting for total time used at a level (new Rule 4).

Why do higher MLFQ queues get shorter time slices?

They hold interactive jobs that need fast switching; lower queues hold CPU-bound jobs that benefit from long slices with less switching.

Lottery vs stride scheduling?

Lottery picks a random ticket each slice — simple, no global state, fair on average. Stride is deterministic (run lowest pass, add stride) — exactly fair but needs global state.

How does Linux CFS pick the next process?

The one with the lowest virtual runtime, stored in a red-black tree; nice values weight how fast vruntime grows.

Single-queue vs multi-queue multiprocessor scheduling?

Single-queue: simple, balanced, but lock contention and poor cache affinity. Multi-queue: scalable and affinity-friendly, but needs migration/work stealing to fix load imbalance.
