docs.title: L06 · Address spaces & the memory API
docs.text:
Book: Ch 13 (pp. 113–121) 🔴 · Ch 14 (pp. 123–133) 🟡 · Time: 30 min · Tool: valgrind

In plain words

Every process gets its own private map of memory, like every flat in a building having rooms numbered "1, 2, 3…". Two flats can both have a "room 3"; they're different rooms. The building manager (OS + hardware) knows which real room each one is.

On that map, the program's code sits at the bottom. The heap (memory you ask for while running) grows upward, and the stack (local variables) grows downward from the top. They grow toward each other into the free space in the middle.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• The address space is the process's private view of memory: code at the bottom, then heap growing up, stack at the top growing down.
  • Every address a program sees is virtual. The OS + hardware translate it to a physical address.
  • Goals of virtual memory: transparency, efficiency, protection. Stack memory is automatic; heap memory is malloc/free and is where the bugs live.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can the OS build the abstraction of a private, possibly large address space for many processes, all sharing one physical memory?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Early machines: one program in memory → ❌ CPU idle while waiting for I/O → multiprogramming: several programs in memory, switch between them → time sharing: interactive users → ❌ saving whole memory to disk on each switch is far too slow → leave everyone in memory at once → ❌ now one process can read or overwrite another → give each process an address space, translated and protected by hardware.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph AS["Address space (virtual) — 0 KB to 16 KB example"]
        direction TB
        Code["0 KB · Program code"]
        Heap["Heap · malloc'd data<br/>⬇ grows to higher addresses"]
        Free["… free …"]
        Stack["Stack · locals, args, return addresses<br/>⬆ grows to lower addresses · ends at 16 KB"]
        Code --- Heap --- Free --- Stack
    end

Read it top to bottom as addresses going up, from 0 KB to 16 KB:

  • Code sits at the start and never changes size.
  • The heap starts just after it and grows up as the program calls malloc.
  • The stack starts at the very end and grows down with each function call.

The heap and stack grow toward each other, so either one can use the free space in the middle. Real address spaces are much bigger (gigabytes), but the shape is the same.

docs.title: The three goals
docs.text:
Goal Meaning Transparency Programs behave as if they had their own real memory; they never notice the trick Efficiency Translating addresses must be fast (the hardware helps, e.g. the TLB), and the OS's bookkeeping must not eat much memory Protection A process can't read or change another process's memory, or the OS's. This is called isolation

Every address you can see in a program is virtual. If you print the address of a variable (printf("%p", &x) in C), you get a virtual address, not a real location in RAM.

docs.title: Memory API (Ch 14)
docs.text:
C programs get memory in two ways:

  • Stack memory is automatic. Write int x; inside a function and the space appears; when the function returns, it's gone. You never free it yourself.
  • Heap memory is manual. int *p = malloc(10 * sizeof(int)); asks for room for 10 integers and gives you its address in p. You must later call free(p); to give it back. (In Java or Python, the garbage collector does the freeing for you.)
  • sizeof(int) is "how many bytes an int needs", so you don't hard-code the number. For text, ask for strlen(s) + 1 bytes: C strings end with a hidden zero byte ('\0') that needs room too.
  • malloc and free are library functions, not system calls. The library manages a pool of heap memory itself, and only asks the OS for a bigger pool now and then (using the system calls brk/sbrk, which move the end of the heap, or mmap).
  • Related calls: calloc (like malloc, but zeroes the memory) and realloc (make an allocation bigger or smaller).

docs.title: The classic heap bugs
docs.text:
Bug What happens Forgetting to allocate Writing through a pointer that points nowhere → crash (segmentation fault, "segfault") Not allocating enough Writing past the end (buffer overflow) — may seem to work, may corrupt other data, and is a classic security hole Forgetting to initialise Reading memory you never set → random leftover values Forgetting to free Memory leak — memory use grows and grows; deadly in programs that run for days Freeing too early Dangling pointer — you still use memory that's been handed back and may be reused Freeing twice Double free — confuses the allocator; anything can happen Freeing a bad pointer Invalid free — passing free an address malloc never gave you

When the process exits, the OS reclaims all its memory anyway — leaks matter in long-running programs and the OS itself.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• malloc is not a system call.
  • sizeof(p) on a pointer gives the pointer size (8 bytes), not the array size.
  • "It ran without crashing" doesn't mean it's correct — use valgrind or AddressSanitizer.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: draw the address space with code/heap/stack and growth directions; list the three goals; list five heap bugs.

What are the three segments of a typical address space and how do they grow?

Code (fixed), heap (grows towards higher addresses), stack (grows towards lower addresses).

What are the three goals of virtual memory?

Transparency, efficiency (time and space), protection/isolation.

Is malloc() a system call?

No. It's a library routine; it gets memory from the OS with brk/sbrk or mmap.

Why must you allocate strlen(s)+1 bytes to copy a string?

To leave room for the terminating null byte.

What is a dangling pointer?

A pointer to memory that has already been freed; using it is undefined behaviour.

docs.title: L07 · Address translation: base/bounds & segmentation
docs.text:
Book: Ch 15 (pp. 135–148) · Ch 16 (pp. 149–160) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 45 min · Simulators: vm-mechanism/relocation.py, vm-segmentation/segmentation.py

In plain words

Every address a program uses has to be turned into a real memory address, on every single access, so it must be cheap.

  • Base and bounds: "Your flat is the block of rooms starting at room 32,000 (base), and it's 16 rooms long (bounds). Room 5 for you = real room 32,005. Ask for room 20 and you're stopped."
  • Segmentation: the same, but the code, heap and stack each get their own base and bounds, so the empty space between heap and stack doesn't waste real memory.
  • The catch: pieces of different sizes leave awkward gaps in memory, like a car park where cars of every length come and go.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Base and bounds (dynamic relocation): physical = virtual + base; if virtual ≥ bounds, raise an exception. Two registers in the MMU, changed only in kernel mode.
  • It wastes the free space between heap and stack (internal fragmentation) — so give each segment (code, heap, stack) its own base/bounds pair: segmentation.
  • Segmentation leaves variable-sized holes in physical memory (external fragmentation) → paging (L09).

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we virtualize memory efficiently and flexibly, while keeping control over which addresses each process can touch?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Need translation on every access, fast → hardware-based dynamic relocation: base + bounds per process → ❌ the whole address space must be contiguous in memory, and the unused middle (between heap and stack) wastes physical memory → one base/bounds pair per segment (segmentation) → add a grows-negative bit for the stack and protection bits for sharing code → ❌ segments are different sizes, so free memory breaks into small holes (external fragmentation); compaction is expensive → paging: fixed-size pieces.

docs.title: Base and bounds
docs.text:
The idea: put each process's whole address space in one continuous chunk of real memory, and give the CPU two registers:

  • base = where the chunk starts in real memory;
  • bounds = how big the chunk is.

On every memory access, the hardware does this:

physical address = virtual address + base
if (virtual address >= bounds) → raise exception (segfault)

The part of the CPU that does this is the MMU (memory management unit). "Raise an exception" means: stop the program and jump into the OS, which usually kills it. That's the familiar "segmentation fault".

What the hardware must provide: user and kernel modes, the base and bounds registers, instructions to change them that only the OS may use (otherwise a program could just point its base at someone else's memory), and a way to raise exceptions.

What the OS must do:

When OS job Process created Find free physical slot (free list), set base/bounds Process exits Put its memory back on the free list Context switch Save/restore base & bounds in the PCB Exception Handle it — usually kill the offending process

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text:
Base and bounds wastes real memory: the whole address space, including the big empty gap between heap and stack, must sit in real memory. Segmentation fixes this by giving each part (segment) of the address space — code, heap, stack — its own base and bounds. Each segment can then sit anywhere in real memory, and the empty gap takes no real memory at all.

Each segment's entry records: base (where it starts in real memory), size (its bounds), which direction it grows (the stack grows down), and protection (may it be read / written / executed?).

How does the hardware know which segment an address belongs to? It uses the top bits of the address. Example: with 14-bit addresses, the top 2 bits say which segment (00 = code, 01 = heap, 11 = stack). The remaining 12 bits are the offset: how far into that segment the address is.

flowchart TB
    VA["Virtual address (14 bits)"] --> S["top 2 bits = segment<br/>00 code · 01 heap · 11 stack"]
    VA --> O["low 12 bits = offset"]
    S --> T["Segment table:<br/>base · bounds · grows+? · prot"]
    O --> CHK{"offset < bounds?"}
    T --> CHK
    CHK -- yes --> PA["physical = base + offset"]
    CHK -- no --> F["segmentation fault"]

The stack is special because it grows downward. Its base marks the top of the stack in real memory, so addresses are counted backwards from there: physical = base + (offset − maximum segment size), which gives a negative distance below the base.

Example: the stack's base is 28 KB, the maximum segment size is 4 KB, and we access offset 3 KB. Then 3 KB − 4 KB = −1 KB, so the physical address is 28 KB − 1 KB = 27 KB.

Sharing: if the code segment is marked read-and-execute only, many processes running the same program can safely share one copy of it in real memory.

Coarse vs fine-grained: most systems use a few big segments (code, heap, stack). Some early systems (Multics) used thousands of small ones, which needs a segment table stored in memory.

docs.title: The OS problem: external fragmentation
docs.text:
Segments come in different sizes. As processes start and stop, real memory fills with odd-sized holes, which is external fragmentation. You might have 20 KB free in total but no single hole bigger than 5 KB.

Options: compaction (stop processes and slide segments together to merge the holes — slow), or a smarter way of choosing holes (L08). Neither solves it completely, which is why the next idea, paging, uses pieces that are all the same size.

docs.title: Worked example (base & bounds)
docs.text:
A process's 16 KB address space is loaded at real address 32 KB. So base = 32 KB = 32768 and bounds = 16 KB = 16384. For each virtual address, check it's below the bounds, then add the base:

Virtual Check Physical 0 0 < 16384 ✔ 32768 1 KB (1024) ✔ 33792 3000 ✔ 35768 4400 ✔ 37168 16384 ✘ fault

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Bounds holds the size (check before adding base) in the book's version; some versions store the physical end. Be explicit in your answer.
  • Base/bounds wastes memory inside the address space (internal); segmentation wastes memory between segments (external).
  • The stack's negative-offset calculation is a favourite exam question — practise it.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the base/bounds formula; four OS duties; the segmentation translation diagram; the stack formula.

How does base-and-bounds translation work?

Physical = virtual + base; if virtual ≥ bounds, the hardware raises an exception.

Where do base and bounds live, and who can change them?

In the CPU's MMU; only privileged (kernel-mode) instructions can change them. The OS saves/restores them in the PCB on a context switch.

What problem does segmentation solve over base-and-bounds?

It avoids wasting physical memory for the unused space between heap and stack, by relocating each segment separately.

How does the hardware know which segment a virtual address is in?

Typically the top bits of the virtual address select the segment; the rest is the offset.

What is external fragmentation and why does segmentation cause it?

Free memory split into many small variable-sized holes. Segments have different sizes, so allocating and freeing them leaves gaps too small to use.

How are code segments shared between processes?

With protection bits: a read-execute-only code segment can be mapped into many address spaces safely.

docs.title: L08 · Free-space management
docs.text:
Book: Ch 17 (pp. 161–177) · Priority: 🟡 good to know · Time: 25 min · Simulator: vm-freespace/malloc.py

In plain words

Like a car park with no marked spaces. Cars (memory requests) of every length arrive and leave. When one leaves, it leaves a gap. The attendant (malloc) must decide where each new car goes:

  • Best fit: the smallest gap that fits.
  • First fit: the first gap that fits.
  • Worst fit: the biggest gap.

Each choice leaves different leftover gaps. The attendant also merges neighbouring gaps (coalescing), and each car carries a small tag saying how long it is (the header).

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• A free list tracks holes. To allocate, split a hole; on free, coalesce with neighbours.
  • Each allocated block carries a small header (size + magic number) just before the pointer you get back, so free(ptr) knows the size.
  • Policies: best fit, worst fit, first fit, next fit. Smarter tricks: segregated lists / slab allocator, buddy allocation. All trade speed for fragmentation; none is perfect.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How should we manage variable-sized free space to minimise fragmentation, and what do the time/space trade-offs look like?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Variable-sized requests → keep a list of free chunks → split a chunk to satisfy a request → ❌ after frees, the list has many small adjacent chunks → coalesce neighbours on free → ❌ free(ptr) gets no size → store a header in front of each block → ❌ which hole to pick? → fit policies → ❌ searching is slow and still fragments → segregated lists for popular sizes (slab), buddy for fast coalescing.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text: This lesson is about how malloc and free manage the heap. (The same problem appears wherever variable-size pieces are handed out, e.g. segments in L07.) The allocator keeps a free list: a list of the holes it can still hand out.

docs.title: Mechanisms (how it works)
docs.text:
• Splitting: asked for 1 byte from a 10-byte hole, hand out 1 byte and keep the other 9 as a smaller hole.
  • Coalescing: when a chunk is freed and its neighbours are free too, merge them into one bigger hole. Otherwise memory ends up as lots of tiny holes.
  • The header: free(p) is only given an address, not a size, so how does it know how much to free? malloc secretly reserves a few extra bytes just before the address it returns, and writes the size there (plus a "magic number" to detect mistakes). free looks just before p to read it. So a request for N bytes really uses N + header bytes.
  • Where does the free list live? Inside the free memory itself. Each hole begins with a small note: "I'm this big, and the next hole is over there".
  • Running out: if no hole is big enough, the allocator asks the OS to make the heap bigger (sbrk).

docs.title: Policies (which hole to pick)
docs.text: Policy Rule Pro Con Best fit Smallest hole that fits Little waste per allocation Full search; leaves tiny unusable slivers Worst fit Largest hole Leaves big leftovers Full search; studies show it fragments badly First fit First hole that fits Fast Small slivers pile up at the start of the list Next fit First fit, starting where last search ended Spreads allocations Similar to first fit

docs.title: Other approaches
docs.text:
• Segregated lists / slab allocator (used inside the Solaris and Linux kernels): if a program keeps asking for the same few sizes, keep a separate ready-made stock of each, like a café pre-cutting sandwiches into the sizes people always order. Very fast, and little fragmentation.
  • Buddy allocator: memory comes in power-of-two sizes (64, 32, 16, 8 KB…). For a request, keep halving a block until the next halving would be too small. Each half has a twin, its buddy. When a block is freed, check whether its buddy is free too; if so, merge them back into the bigger block, and repeat upward. Merging is quick, but requests are rounded up to a power of two, so space is wasted inside blocks (internal fragmentation). In the picture, a 7 KB request gets an 8 KB block and 1 KB is wasted.
flowchart TB
    A["64 KB"] --> B["32 KB"] & C["32 KB"]
    B --> D["16 KB"] & E["16 KB"]
    D --> F["8 KB ✅ allocated for a 7 KB request"] & G["8 KB free (buddy)"]

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Internal fragmentation = waste inside an allocated block (buddy rounding). External = waste between blocks (holes).
  • malloc(N) uses more than N bytes because of the header.
  • Best fit isn't automatically best — it leaves tiny slivers.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: splitting, coalescing, header, four fit policies with one con each, slab and buddy in one line each.

How does free() know the size of the block?

It reads a header stored just before the returned pointer, which holds the size (and a magic number for integrity).

What is coalescing?

Merging a freed chunk with adjacent free chunks into a single larger free chunk.

Best fit vs first fit?

Best fit searches the whole list for the smallest hole that fits (less waste, slow, slivers). First fit takes the first hole that fits (fast, slivers at the list head).

How does the buddy allocator make coalescing easy?

Blocks are powers of two; a block's buddy address differs by a single bit, so checking and merging is quick and recursive.

What's the main downside of the buddy allocator?

Internal fragmentation, because requests are rounded up to a power of two.

docs.title: L09 · Paging
docs.text:
Book: Ch 18 (pp. 179–191) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 45 min · Simulator: vm-paging/paging-linear-translate.py

In plain words

Instead of storing a program in one big piece, chop its memory into equal-size pages (usually 4 KB), like pages of a book. Real memory is chopped into page-size slots called frames. Any page can go in any free frame.

Each process has a page table: an index saying "page 0 is in frame 7, page 1 is in frame 3, …". An address is just "page number + position inside the page". The hardware looks up the page number in the table, swaps in the frame number, and keeps the position unchanged.

The problem: that index is big, and looking in it on every access is slow. The next two lessons fix both.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Split the virtual address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size page frames. No external fragmentation, and sparse address spaces are easy.
  • Virtual address = VPN (virtual page number) + offset. A per-process page table maps VPN → PFN; the offset is copied unchanged.
  • Two problems: page tables are big (4 MB per process on 32-bit with 4 KB pages) and paging is slow (an extra memory access per access). Fixes: TLB (L10) and smaller tables (L11).

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we virtualize memory with pages, avoiding segmentation's problems? What are the basic techniques, and how do we make them work with minimal space and time overhead?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Segments fragment memory → chop everything into fixed-size pages → page table per process: VPN → PFN → ❌ page table is huge → keep it in memory, find it via a page-table base register → ❌ every load/store now needs an extra memory access to read the page table → ❌ too slow → TLB; ❌ too big → multi-level tables.

docs.title: Splitting the address
docs.text:
Every virtual address is read as two parts:

  • VPN (virtual page number): which page.
  • Offset: where inside that page.

It's like a street address "flat 12, room 3": flat number and room number. In binary, the split is easy. If a page holds 2k bytes, the lowest k bits are the offset and the remaining high bits are the VPN.

Tiny example: a 64-byte address space (6-bit addresses) with 16-byte pages has 64 ÷ 16 = 4 pages.

  • 4 pages need 2 bits to number them (00, 01, 10, 11), so the VPN is 2 bits.
  • 16 bytes per page need 4 bits (0–15), so the offset is 4 bits.
  • Virtual address 21 in binary is 01 0101 → VPN = 01 = page 1, offset = 0101 = byte 5 of that page.

Then the page table (one per process, stored in memory) says which real frame holds that page. The frame number (PFN, physical frame number) replaces the VPN; the offset stays exactly the same.

flowchart TB
    VA["Virtual address<br/>VPN | offset"] --> PT["Page table[VPN]<br/>(via page-table base register)"]
    PT --> PTE["PTE: PFN · valid · prot · present · dirty · ref"]
    PTE --> PA["Physical address<br/>PFN | offset"]
    VA -- offset copied unchanged --> PA

docs.title: What's in a page-table entry (PTE)
docs.text:
Bit Purpose PFN Physical frame number Valid Is this part of the address space at all? (unused pages invalid → no frame needed) Protection Read / write / execute Present In memory or swapped to disk? (L12) Dirty Modified since loaded? Reference / accessed Used recently? (for replacement) User/supervisor Can user mode touch it?

The simplest page table is a linear page table: a plain array where entry number n describes page n.

docs.title: The translation steps (in hardware)
docs.text:
In words: split off the VPN → find that entry in the page table (one memory read) → check the page is valid and allowed → glue the frame number onto the unchanged offset → do the real memory access. As pseudo-code:

VPN     = (VirtualAddress & VPN_MASK) >> SHIFT
PTEAddr = PTBR + (VPN * sizeof(PTE))
PTE     = AccessMemory(PTEAddr)          ← the extra access
if (PTE.Valid == False)        → raise SEGMENTATION_FAULT
else if (!CanAccess(PTE.Prot)) → raise PROTECTION_FAULT
else
    offset   = VirtualAddress & OFFSET_MASK
    PhysAddr = (PTE.PFN << SHIFT) | offset
    Register = AccessMemory(PhysAddr)
  • & with a MASK keeps only certain bits; >> SHIFT slides them right. Together they pull the VPN out of the address.
  • PTBR (page-table base register) holds where this process's page table starts in memory. Entry n is at PTBR + n × (size of one entry).
  • << SHIFT and | put the frame number back in the high bits, next to the offset.
  • Notice there are two memory accesses: one to read the PTE and one for the real data. That's why plain paging is slow.

docs.title: Numbers to remember
docs.text:
• The 4 MB problem, step by step: with 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, the offset needs 12 bits (4 KB = 212), leaving 20 bits of VPN. That's 220 ≈ 1 million possible pages, so 1 million page-table entries. At 4 bytes each, that's 4 MB of page table for every process. With 100 processes, 400 MB of memory holds nothing but page tables.
  • Paging doubles memory accesses without a TLB (one for the PTE, one for the data). An instruction fetch also needs translation.

docs.title: Worked example (do it)
docs.text:
32 KB address space, 4 KB pages, physical memory 128 KB.

  • Pages in address space = 32/4 = 8 → VPN is 3 bits; offset is 12 bits; virtual address is 15 bits.
  • Physical frames = 128/4 = 32 → PFN is 5 bits; physical address 17 bits.
  • Virtual address 0x3229 = binary 011 0010 0010 1001 → VPN 3, offset 0x229. If PT[3] = PFN 7 → physical = 7 << 12 | 0x229 = 0x7229.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• The offset is not translated — only the VPN changes.
  • Count bits from sizes: offset bits = log2(page size); VPN bits = log2(address space / page size).
  • Valid bit ≠ present bit. Invalid = not part of the address space (fault → kill). Not present = swapped out (page fault → load it).
  • Page tables live in memory (kernel space), not in the MMU.

docs.text:

What is a page vs a page frame?

A page is a fixed-size chunk of virtual memory; a page frame is the same-size slot in physical memory.

How is a virtual address split under paging?

High bits = virtual page number (VPN); low log2(page size) bits = offset.

Which part of the address does the page table translate?

Only the VPN → PFN. The offset is copied unchanged.

How large is a linear page table for a 32-bit space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte PTEs?

2^20 entries × 4 bytes = 4 MB per process.

Why is basic paging slow?

Each memory reference needs an extra memory access to fetch the PTE first.

Valid bit vs present bit?

Valid: the page belongs to the address space. Present: the page is currently in physical memory (not swapped out).

Two advantages of paging over segmentation?

No external fragmentation (all frames same size), and flexible support for sparse address spaces.

docs.title: L10 · TLBs: making paging fast
docs.text:
Book: Ch 19 (pp. 193–209) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 40 min

In plain words

Looking up the page table on every memory access is like checking the phone book every time you call a friend. The TLB is your speed-dial: a tiny list of the few translations you used most recently, built into the CPU. Most of the time the number is on speed-dial (a hit) and you skip the phone book.

It works because programs keep touching the same few pages (locality).

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• The TLB (translation-lookaside buffer) is a small, fast hardware cache of VPN → PFN translations inside the MMU. A hit skips the page-table access.
  • It works because of locality: spatial (nearby addresses share a page) and temporal (the same page is used again soon).
  • Context switches make old entries wrong: either flush the TLB or tag entries with an ASID (address-space ID).

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we speed up address translation and avoid the extra memory reference paging needs?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Paging needs an extra memory access per access → cache translations in hardware: the TLB → ❌ on a miss someone must walk the page table → hardware-managed (x86) or software-managed (MIPS: trap to OS) → ❌ after a context switch, entries belong to the wrong process → flush on switch → ❌ flushing throws away useful entries → tag entries with an ASID → ❌ TLB is full → replacement: LRU or random.

docs.title: The TLB control flow
docs.text:
On every memory access, the hardware first checks the TLB. Hit: the translation is there, so use it and you're done, with no extra memory access. Miss: look in the page table the slow way, copy the answer into the TLB, and try the instruction again. This time it hits.

flowchart TB
    A[Extract VPN] --> B{TLB hit?}
    B -- yes --> C{Protection OK?}
    C -- yes --> D["PA = PFN | offset → access memory"]
    C -- no --> E[Protection fault]
    B -- no --> F["Walk page table (1 extra memory access)"]
    F --> G{PTE valid?}
    G -- no --> H[Segfault]
    G -- yes --> I["Insert into TLB, retry instruction"]
    I --> A

docs.title: Locality example
docs.text:
A loop reads an array of 10 integers (4 bytes each) that starts at virtual address 100. Pages are tiny here, 16 bytes, so one page holds 4 integers and the array covers 3 pages.

  • Reading a[0] → its page isn't in the TLB yet: miss. The translation is now cached.
  • a[1], a[2] → same page: hit, hit.
  • a[3] → new page: miss; then a[4]–a[6]: hit, hit, hit.
  • a[7] → new page: miss; then a[8], a[9]: hit, hit.

That's 3 misses and 7 hits, a 70% hit rate, purely because neighbouring elements share a page (spatial locality). With real 4 KB pages, 1,000 integers fit per page, so the hit rate would be over 99.9%. Run the loop a second time and everything hits, because the pages were used recently (temporal locality).

docs.title: Who handles a miss?
docs.text:
On a TLB miss, someone has to look in the page table. Two designs exist:

Hardware does it (e.g. Intel/AMD x86) The OS does it (e.g. MIPS) On a miss The CPU walks the page table itself, using a register that holds the table's address (CR3 on x86) The CPU raises an exception; OS code finds the entry and loads it into the TLB with a special instruction Page-table layout Must be exactly what the hardware expects The OS can store page tables any way it likes Watch out — After handling the miss, the OS must re-run the instruction that missed (not skip to the next one). And the miss-handling code must not itself cause a TLB miss, or it would loop forever

docs.title: A TLB entry
docs.text:
Each TLB entry holds a VPN, the matching PFN, and a few flag bits (valid, protection, ASID, dirty…). Any entry can hold any translation, and the hardware searches all of them at once (fully associative). TLBs are tiny: typically 32 to 128 entries.

Don't mix up the two "valid" bits: in the TLB, valid means "this slot holds a translation"; in the page table, valid means "this page is part of the program's address space".

docs.title: Context switches
docs.text:
Problem: process A's "page 10" and process B's "page 10" are different pages. After switching from A to B, the TLB still holds A's translations, and B would use them by mistake.

  • Option 1 — flush: empty the TLB on every switch. Correct, but each process restarts with an empty TLB and many misses.
  • Option 2 — ASID (address-space identifier): label every entry with which process it belongs to, like a name tag. The TLB only uses entries whose label matches the current process, so entries for several processes can live side by side.

docs.title: Replacement
docs.text: When the TLB is full, which entry gets replaced? Either the least recently used one (LRU — works well thanks to locality) or a random one. Random sounds silly but is simple and avoids LRU's worst case: a loop over 65 pages with a 64-entry TLB, where LRU always throws out exactly the entry needed next.

docs.title: Numbers to remember
docs.text:
• TLB hit takes ~1 cycle; a miss costs one or more memory accesses (hundreds of cycles with multi-level tables).
  • TLB coverage = entries × page size. 64 entries × 4 KB = 256 KB. Programs touching more than that pages miss a lot → huge pages (2 MB/1 GB) help databases.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• The TLB caches translations, not data. (The CPU caches hold data.)
  • Software-managed TLB miss handler: return-from-trap must re-execute the faulting instruction.
  • "RAM isn't always RAM": randomly accessing more pages than the TLB covers can be far slower than you expect.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the hit/miss flowchart; the array example's hit rate; hardware vs software miss handling; flush vs ASID.

What does the TLB store?

Recently used virtual-to-physical page translations (VPN → PFN plus protection and other bits).

Why does the TLB work well for most programs?

Spatial and temporal locality: nearby accesses fall in the same page and pages get reused.

Hardware-managed vs software-managed TLB miss?

Hardware: the CPU walks the page table itself (x86). Software: the CPU traps to the OS, which walks the table and installs the entry (MIPS) — more flexible.

What's special about returning from a TLB-miss trap?

It must retry the instruction that caused the miss, unlike a syscall return which continues with the next instruction.

How do ASIDs help with context switches?

Entries are tagged with the address-space ID, so the TLB can hold translations for several processes without flushing.

What is TLB coverage?

Number of entries × page size — the amount of memory reachable without a TLB miss.

docs.title: L11 · Smaller page tables: multi-level & friends
docs.text:
Book: Ch 20 (pp. 211–226) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Time: 45 min · Simulator: vm-smalltables/paging-multilevel-translate.py

In plain words

A simple page table has one entry for every possible page, even though most of a program's address range is empty. It's like a 1,000-page phone book where 990 pages are blank.

A multi-level page table is a phone book with a table of contents (the page directory). The contents page says which sections exist, and empty sections are simply not printed. You save a lot of paper. The cost is one extra lookup (contents, then section), and the TLB hides that most of the time.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Linear page tables waste memory on invalid entries for the huge unused middle of the address space.
  • Multi-level page table: chop the page table into page-sized pieces; a page directory points only to the pieces that have valid entries. Unused regions cost nothing.
  • Cost: a TLB miss now needs one memory access per level (time–space trade-off). Alternatives: bigger pages, paging+segments hybrid, inverted page tables.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can we make page tables smaller, without making translation too slow?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

4 MB of page table per process, mostly invalid entries → bigger pages (16 KB → 1 MB table) → ❌ internal fragmentation, waste inside pages → hybrid: a page table per segment, with bounds → ❌ still needs segmentation, tables are variable-sized again (external fragmentation) → multi-level: page the page table itself → ❌ more memory accesses on a TLB miss, more complex → accept it, because the TLB hits most of the time → x86-64 uses 4 levels.

docs.title: Two-level page table
docs.text:
Take the big page table and cut it into page-sized pieces. Then add a small top-level index, the page directory, with one entry per piece. Each entry says either "this piece exists, and it's at frame X" or "this piece is all empty, so it isn't stored at all".

The VPN is now read in two parts: the first part picks the entry in the page directory, the second part picks the entry inside that piece.

flowchart TB
    VA["VPN = PD index | PT index ,  offset"] --> PDBR["Page-directory base register"]
    PDBR --> PD["Page directory<br/>PDE: valid + PFN of a page of PTEs"]
    PD -- PDE valid --> PTP["One page of the page table"]
    PD -. PDE invalid → whole chunk unmapped, no page allocated .-> X[ ]
    PTP --> PTE["PTE → PFN"]
    PTE --> PA["PFN | offset"]
  • Each page-directory entry (PDE) covers one page-sized piece of the page table. If the PDE is marked invalid, that piece isn't allocated at all. This is where the savings come from.
  • Every piece is exactly one page in size, so the OS can store it in any free frame: no fragmentation, and pieces can even be moved out to disk.

docs.title: Translation on a TLB miss (two levels)
docs.text:
In words: use the top part of the VPN to read the page-directory entry (memory read 1) → if valid, it tells you which frame holds the right piece → use the next part of the VPN to read the PTE inside that piece (memory read 2) → put the result in the TLB and retry.

PDIndex = (VPN & PD_MASK) >> PD_SHIFT
PDE     = Memory[PDBR + PDIndex * sizeof(PDE)]       ← access 1
if PDE.Valid:
    PTIndex = VPN & PT_MASK
    PTE     = Memory[(PDE.PFN << SHIFT) + PTIndex * sizeof(PTE)]   ← access 2
    if PTE.Valid → insert in TLB, retry

docs.title: How many levels?
docs.text:
Rule: every piece (including the top directory) must fit in one page.

  • A 4 KB page holds 4096 ÷ 4 = 1024 entries of 4 bytes. Choosing one of 1024 entries takes 10 bits, so each level uses 10 bits of the VPN.
  • 32-bit machine: 32 bits − 12 offset bits = 20 VPN bits = 10 + 10 → 2 levels (classic 32-bit x86).
  • 64-bit machine (uses 48-bit addresses, 8-byte entries): 4096 ÷ 8 = 512 entries per page → 9 bits per level. 48 − 12 = 36 VPN bits = 4 × 9 → 4 levels (today's x86-64).

docs.title: The other options (one line each)
docs.text: Option Idea Downside Bigger pages Fewer pages means fewer entries Small programs waste most of each big page (internal fragmentation) Hybrid (paging + segments) A separate page table for code, heap and stack, each only as long as needed Inflexible; tables of different sizes bring fragmentation back Inverted page table One table for the whole machine, with one entry per real frame saying which process and page is in it; found quickly with a hash table Every lookup needs a search; sharing pages is awkward Swap page tables to disk Page tables can themselves be paged out Complex (VAX/VMS did this)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A small machine: 16 KB address space, tiny 64-byte pages.

  1. Count the pages: 16 KB ÷ 64 B = 256 pages, so the VPN is 8 bits (28 = 256) and the offset is 6 bits (26 = 64).
  2. Size of a simple linear table: 256 entries × 4 bytes = 1 KB. That's 1 KB ÷ 64 B = 16 pages of page table, each holding 16 entries.
  3. Make it two-level: the directory needs one entry per piece, so 16 entries, chosen by the top 4 bits of the VPN. The next 4 bits choose the entry inside a piece.
  4. What's actually used? Say the program only uses code (pages 0–1), heap (pages 4–5) and stack (pages 254–255). Pages 0–15 fall in piece #0, and pages 240–255 fall in piece #15. The other 14 pieces are completely empty and are never allocated.
  5. Result: 1 directory page + 2 pieces = 3 pages instead of 16.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• The page directory itself must fit in one page — otherwise add a level.
  • More levels = smaller tables but more accesses per TLB miss; no extra cost on a TLB hit.
  • Inverted tables are indexed by physical frame, not virtual page.

docs.text:

Why are linear page tables wasteful?

They allocate a PTE for every virtual page, even the vast unused region between heap and stack.

How does a multi-level page table save space?

The page table is split into page-sized chunks; a page directory tracks them, and chunks with no valid entries are never allocated.

What's the cost of a two-level page table?

On a TLB miss, two memory accesses instead of one to translate (plus more complexity).

How many 4-byte PTEs fit in a 4 KB page, and what does that imply?

1024 → each level indexes with 10 bits.

What's an inverted page table?

A single system-wide table with one entry per physical frame, recording which process and virtual page use it; searched with a hash table.

Why not just use bigger pages?

Internal fragmentation: most of each big page goes unused for small allocations.

docs.title: L12 · Swapping: going beyond physical memory
docs.text:
Book: Ch 21 (pp. 227–235) · Ch 22 (pp. 237–254) · Priority: 🔴 must-know · Ch 23 ⚪ · Time: 55 min · Simulator: vm-beyondphys-policy/paging-policy.py

In plain words

Your desk (RAM) is small; the filing cabinet (disk) is huge but slow. When your desk is full and you need another folder:

  • Mechanism: each page's entry has a "present?" flag. If a program touches a page that's in the cabinet, the hardware raises a page fault, and the OS fetches it from disk.
  • Policy: which folder do you put back to make room? Ideally the one you'll need furthest in the future (OPT). Since nobody knows the future, the usual guess is "the one you haven't touched for the longest" (LRU), or a cheap approximation of it (Clock).

If you need more folders than fit on the desk at once, you spend all day walking to the cabinet. That's thrashing.

docs.title: TL;DR (the 3 things to remember)
docs.text:
• Mechanism: pages can live in swap space on disk. The PTE's present bit says whether a page is in memory. Touching a non-present page → page fault → the OS reads it from disk, updates the PTE, retries.
  • Policy: when memory is full, evict a page. OPT (evict the page used furthest in the future) is the unbeatable benchmark; LRU approximates it using history; Clock approximates LRU cheaply with a use bit.
  • If the working sets don't fit, the system thrashes. Evicting clean pages is cheaper than dirty ones.

docs.title: The big question
docs.text: How can the OS use a larger, slower device to give the illusion of a large virtual memory — and how does it decide which page to evict?

docs.title: The story chain
docs.text:
Key: bold = the problem or the final design · italics = an attempted fix · ❌ = what goes wrong with it · → = "which leads to"

Address spaces larger than RAM → store some pages on disk; present bit in the PTE → page fault handler loads the page → ❌ memory full → evict something → which? OPT → ❌ needs the future → FIFO → ❌ ignores importance, and suffers Belady's anomaly → Random → ❌ luck-based → LRU, uses history → ❌ exact LRU means updating a data structure on every memory access → Clock: a use bit set by hardware, a sweeping hand → prefer clean pages; evict in the background with a swap daemon → ❌ too many processes for memory → admission control or the OOM killer.

docs.title: The page-fault path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Process
    participant HW as MMU / TLB
    participant OS as OS page-fault handler
    participant D as Disk (swap)
    P->>HW: load from virtual address
    HW->>HW: TLB miss → walk table<br/>PTE valid, present = 0
    HW->>OS: page fault
    OS->>OS: find a free frame<br/>(or evict one, write it out if dirty)
    OS->>D: read page from swap (disk address in the PTE)
    Note over P,OS: process is Blocked, another one runs
    D-->>OS: I/O complete
    OS->>OS: PTE.present = 1, PTE.PFN = frame
    OS->>P: retry instruction → TLB miss → TLB hit

How to read the diagram: the program touches a page; the hardware finds its "present" flag is 0 and calls the OS (a page fault); the OS finds room, reads the page from disk (the process sleeps meanwhile and others run), marks it present and re-runs the instruction.

Note the difference from L09: a page that is not valid isn't part of the program at all, so touching it is a bug and the program is killed. A page that is valid but not present is legitimate; it's just on disk right now.

When are pages evicted? Not at the last moment. A background OS thread (the swap daemon) wakes up when free memory drops below a low watermark and evicts pages in a batch until free memory reaches a high watermark. Batching is faster because several pages can be written to disk together.

docs.title: Average memory access time
docs.text:
AMAT = TM + Pmiss × TD

In words: every access costs one memory access (TM), plus — for the fraction of accesses that miss (Pmiss) — a trip to disk (TD).

Example: memory takes 100 ns; disk takes 10 ms, which is 10,000,000 ns.

  • 90% hits (Pmiss = 0.1): 100 ns + 0.1 × 10,000,000 ns ≈ 1 ms per access — 10,000× slower than memory.
  • 99.9% hits (Pmiss = 0.001): 100 ns + 10,000 ns ≈ 10.1 µs — still 100× slower than memory.

Lesson: disk is so slow that even a tiny miss rate dominates. Swapping is a safety net, not something to rely on.

docs.title: The policies (which page to throw out)
docs.text:
Here RAM acts as a cache for the disk. A hit means the page was already in memory; a miss (page fault) means it had to be fetched from disk. To evict a page means to remove it from memory to make room.

Policy Evicts Notes OPT (optimal, by Belady) The page that won't be needed for the longest time The best possible, but needs to know the future. Used only as a benchmark for the others FIFO The page that arrived first Simple, but may throw out a page in constant use. Strange quirk (Belady's anomaly): giving it more memory can cause more misses Random Any page, at random Simple; no bad worst case, but no cleverness either LRU The page not used for the longest time Usually good, because recently used pages tend to be used again. Never shows Belady's anomaly LFU The page used the fewest times Same spirit as LRU, counting uses instead of recency Clock See below A cheap approximation of LRU, used in real systems

How Clock works: imagine the pages arranged in a circle, with a clock hand pointing at one. The hardware sets a page's use bit to 1 whenever it's accessed. To evict, look at the page under the hand. If its use bit is 1, it was used recently: give it a second chance (set the bit to 0) and move on. If its use bit is 0, it hasn't been used since the hand last passed, so evict it. A common variant also prefers pages that haven't been modified (clean pages), because those don't need writing back to disk first.

docs.title: Workload lessons
docs.text:
How well a policy does depends on the program's access pattern:

  • Random accesses (no locality): every realistic policy does the same; only the amount of memory matters.
  • "80-20" pattern (80% of accesses go to 20% of the pages): LRU wins, because it keeps the popular pages.
  • A loop over slightly too many pages (e.g. 51 pages, room for 50): LRU and FIFO miss every single time, because they always evict exactly the page needed next. Random does much better here.

docs.title: Other VM policy bits
docs.text:
• Demand paging: load a page only when it's first touched. Prefetching: guess which page will be needed next and load it early.
  • Thrashing: the pages that running programs actively need (their working sets) don't all fit in memory, so the system spends nearly all its time moving pages to and from disk and gets almost no work done. Fixes: run fewer programs at once (admission control), or kill one (Linux's OOM killer, "out of memory").
  • Two tricks from VAX/VMS (Ch 23):
    • Demand zeroing: when a program asks for a new page, don't clear it yet; clear it only when it's first used (many are never used).
    • Copy-on-write: after fork(), parent and child share their pages instead of copying them all. A page is copied only when one of them writes to it. Since the child usually calls exec() straight away, most pages are never copied, which makes fork + exec cheap.

docs.title: Worked example (do by hand)
docs.text:
A program accesses pages in this order (the reference string): 0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1. Memory has room for 3 pages. For each policy, go through the list: a page already in memory is a hit; otherwise it's a miss, and if memory is full the policy chooses a victim. The first three misses (0, 1, 2) happen no matter what, because memory starts empty (compulsory or cold-start misses).

  • OPT: misses on 0, 1, 2 (cold), 3 (evict 2, used furthest), 2 (evict 3 or 0) → 6 hits / 11 = 54.5% (5 misses, 3 of them compulsory).
  • FIFO: 0 1 2 miss; 0 1 hit; 3 miss (evict 0); 0 miss (evict 1); 3 hit; 1 miss (evict 2); 2 miss (evict 3); 1 hit → 4 hits = 36.4%.
  • LRU: 0 1 2 miss; 0 1 hit; 3 miss (evict 2); 0 3 1 hit; 2 miss (evict 0); 1 hit → 6 hits = 54.5% — matches OPT here.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Valid but not present → page fault (normal). Invalid → segfault.
  • Page faults are handled by the OS even on hardware-managed TLBs (disk I/O needs the OS).
  • LRU has no Belady's anomaly; FIFO does.
  • Evicting a dirty page costs a disk write first.

docs.title: Recall
docs.text:
Blurt test — close this page, then on paper, from memory: the page-fault sequence; AMAT formula with the 99.9% example; the policy table; redo the FIFO trace.

What is the present bit?

A PTE bit saying whether the page is in physical memory (1) or swapped out to disk (0).

What happens on a page fault?

The OS finds a free frame (evicting one if needed), reads the page from swap, sets present=1 and the PFN, and the faulting instruction is retried. The process is blocked during the I/O.

Write the average memory access time formula.

AMAT = T_M + P_miss × T_D.

What does OPT evict and why can't we use it?

The page that will be used furthest in the future; it requires knowing the future.

What is Belady's anomaly?

With FIFO, increasing cache size can increase the number of misses. LRU and OPT (stack algorithms) don't have it.

How does the Clock algorithm work?

Pages in a circle with a hardware-set use bit. The hand sweeps: use bit 1 → clear it and move on; use bit 0 → evict.

Which workload makes LRU and FIFO miss every time?

Looping sequentially over one more page than the cache holds.

What is thrashing and how is it handled?

Memory is oversubscribed so the system spends its time paging. Run fewer processes (admission control) or kill one (OOM killer).

What is copy-on-write?

After fork, parent and child share pages read-only; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it.

Explain it out loud (60 seconds, as if to a friend): "Why does a 99.9% memory hit rate still make a program feel slow if the misses go to disk?"

Simulator drill (book's free Python homework tools — see the recall system): python3 paging-policy.py -p FIFO -a 0,1,2,0,1,3,0,3,1,2,1 -C 3 -c, then -p LRU, -p OPT, -p CLOCK.
